blocks.h: DON’T GIVE WAY TO AMAZEMENT
Roya Publication No. 107
by Chew Z
THE BOOK BEFORE
Each of these books stands on its own, and can be read in any order. The one before this was about a young man named Tomás.

It was a Saturday night in April 2007, in a fraternity house in Los Angeles, and Tomás was twenty years old. For two years he had felt nothing at all. A doctor had given it a name and a prescription. The pills made the flatness quieter, but it was still there, like living behind a window.

That night his friend Danny held up a small printed bag from a smoke shop on the boulevard. People said that what was inside it took the mind to the strangest place it can go. Tomás said yes. If even that could not reach him, he would know.
He made Danny promise to stay sober and hold the camera. The counter began at zero. The last thing Tomás saw before the room folded shut was the small red light on the front of it.
On the other side there was a dirt floor, rain on a tin roof, and a barefoot boy counting leaves in the dark, who had been waiting for him for a very long time.
The next morning Tomás sat with the camera on his knees and watched the whole tape, and told us where he had really been.
SYNOPSIS

Margit Halmos has spent thirty-one years in a glass booth above a hall of the United Nations in Geneva, carrying other people’s words into English half a breath behind them. Delegates, doctors, witnesses at a war-crimes tribunal: if a thing can be said, Margit can say it in another language before the speaker has finished.
In March, a delegate says heron, and Margit says the animal.

A neurologist gives it a name. It is rare and it is slow, and it takes the meanings of words one at a time, the rarest first. It does not stop. In the back of Margit’s notebook, her partner in the booth, Inês, begins a list headed Words gone.

Switzerland lets a person choose the day she dies, but only while her mind is clear enough to choose, and an illness like hers will not wait. Margit joins the association that helps, writes the letter in her own hand, and is given a paper that says she is able. It is good for six months.
Inês has twenty notebooks, every page an attempt to describe twelve minutes in Porto nine years ago. She keeps a small brown bottle at the back of her freezer, and she will not say its name.
For thirty-one years Margit has carried one sentence across the glass more often than any other: there are no words. She has never once asked where the thing goes, the thing there are no words for.
Before her door closes, she means to find out.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

This is a book about an interpreter who is losing the meanings of words, and about a choice that the law of one country offers her, and the trap hidden inside that choice for anyone whose illness is in the mind.

The title comes from Terence McKenna. He said that in the place this book visits, the beings he met told him, more or less, not to stand there gaping: not to give way to amazement, but to look. I have put it in my own words. It seemed to me good advice for anyone standing at any edge, which is where everyone in this book is standing.

The illness is real. It is rare, it is slow, and what it does is described as plainly as I could from the doctors who study it and the families who live with it. The Swiss law is real, and so are the associations that help people use it; the one Margit joins is drawn from their published rules, simplified. The history, the science and the law of the substance are as true as I could make them in 2026. Margit, Inês and every person Margit meets are invented, and so is the journey itself, though it is built from a great many real accounts.
This book does not tell anyone what to choose. The people at the information evening are not wrong, and neither is Margit.
Chew Z
I. THE BOOTH
Words gone this month: heron, ladle, centipede, nephew.
The first word I lost was a bird.

I want to set it down properly, because I have spent my life setting things down properly, and because in a year I will not be able to. It was a Tuesday in March. It was raining on the lake. I was in the booth.

I should tell you what the booth is, since you have probably never sat in one. At the United Nations in Geneva, in the big white building they call the Palais des Nations [pa-LAY day na-SYON], the Palace of Nations, there are rooms where the countries of the world sit in a ring and talk to each other. Above every one of those rooms, behind a long strip of glass, there is a row of small boxes, one for each language. Each box is about the size of a wardrobe. Two people sit in it with headphones on, side by side, and a microphone between them, and a little red light that comes on when you speak.

Down in the room, a man from one country says something in his language. Up in the box, you hear him in your headphones, and at the same moment, half a breath behind him, you say it again in yours. Not after he finishes. While he is speaking. You listen with one ear and speak with your mouth and somewhere in the middle, in the dark between the two, you carry the meaning across, the way you might carry water across a room in your cupped hands and try not to spill.
That is the job. I have done it for thirty-one years. I am, I am told, very good at it. I am not saying this to boast. I am saying it so that you understand how far there is to fall.

On that Tuesday I was in the English booth above Room Twenty. Room Twenty is the one with the ceiling. A Spanish painter covered the whole dome of it with paint that drips down in long points, thousands of them, every colour there is, like the roof of a cave turned inside out, and when the lights come up in the morning the delegates look up at it before they look at each other. I have looked up at it most mornings for seventeen years. I still do not know whether it is beautiful or whether it is about to fall on us.

The delegate from a lake country was speaking about water. A dam upstream, a river that no longer reached a wetland, the birds that used to come there in their thousands. He was speaking French. I was putting him into English. My partner Inês was beside me with her headphones round her neck, eating an apple without making a sound, which is a skill.
And the man said: le héron [luh ay-RON].
And I said: “the animal.”
I heard it come out of my mouth. The animal. Not wrong, exactly. A heron is an animal. But nobody had ever paid me to say that a heron is an animal. They had paid me to say heron.

I kept going. That is the first thing they teach you, and the last thing you forget: you never stop. You never go back. The man is still talking. If you stop to fix one word you lose the next ten. So I went on, the wetland and the dam and the thousands of birds, and my voice was quite steady, and inside my head, very quietly, I was looking for the word.
It was not there.

I don’t mean it was on the tip of my tongue. Everyone knows that feeling, when a word is just behind a door and you can hear it moving about. This was not that. I went to where the word should be and there was nothing behind the door. There was no door. There was a long grey bird standing on one leg in shallow water, very still, the way they stand, with its neck folded like a letter S, and I could see it perfectly. I knew everything about it. I knew that it waits a long time and then strikes. I knew the sound it makes when it takes off, a sort of dry croak, like an old man clearing his throat. I knew that there were three of them on the Rhône [ROHN] by the Pont de la Machine [pon duh la ma-SHEEN] every winter, because I walked past them on my way to the tram.

I just did not know what it was called. In any language. Not in English, not in French, not in Hungarian, which is the language my mother sang to me in. The bird stood there in my mind with no name on it, like a parcel with the label torn off.

At half past eleven Inês touched my arm, which is the signal, and took over without a breath between us, and I took off my headphones and sat back and looked at the ceiling, all those thousands of coloured points hanging over the delegates, and I thought: well.
That was all I thought. Well.
I am going to tell you who I am, while I still can, and then I will not do it again.

My name is Margit Halmos [MAR-git HAL-mosh]. I was born in Budapest in 1971, which means I was born in a country that no longer exists in the form I was born in, which is true of most people in my part of Europe and not something we talk about at parties.

My mother was Hungarian. My father came from Novi Sad [NO-vee sahd], a city on the Danube in what was then Yugoslavia, where half the town spoke Hungarian and half spoke Serbo-Croatian [SUR-bo-kro-AY-shun] and most people spoke both and argued in whichever one was quicker. So I grew up with two languages in the house, one for each parent, and a third one, a sort of private one, that was made of the two of them rubbing together. My mother used to say I learned to translate before I learned to walk, because I was always carrying something one of them had said across the kitchen to the other.
That is not quite true. But it is true enough that I have told it at three funerals, including both of theirs.

I came to Geneva at nineteen to study at the interpreters’ school. I learned English properly, and then French. I married a man who was very kind and very boring and we were not married for long, and neither of us minded much. I have no children. I have a flat in Plainpalais [plan-pa-LAY] with a balcony that looks at another balcony, and a great many books in four languages, and a cat who belongs to the woman downstairs and visits me on Thursdays for reasons of his own.

From 1997 until it closed in 2017, I worked for the war-crimes court in The Hague, the one that was set up to try the men responsible for what happened in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s. I went back and forth between there and Geneva for twenty years. My job there was the same job, in a smaller, colder booth, with worse coffee. A witness would speak in her language, which was my father’s language, and I would carry what she said into English so the judges could hear it.

I worked it out once, on a slow afternoon: in those twenty years I said the word killed out loud, in English, something over eleven thousand times. Other people’s killed. Other people’s dead, carried carefully across the glass to men in robes who wrote them down. I did not cry in the booth. Nobody cries in the booth; you cannot cry and interpret at the same time, the two use the same throat. I cried, when I cried, on the train home. I mention it only so that you know I am not a stranger to death. I have handled more of it than an undertaker. I have simply never had any of my own.

That is who I am. A woman who carries things from one side of a room to the other. I have never had anything of my own to say. I have only ever had other people’s things to carry, and I carried them carefully, and I was proud of not spilling.
The second word went eight days later. It was ladle.

I was cooking. That is the only reason I noticed. In the booth, I might have slid past it; we slide past things all the time. In my kitchen, on my own, I opened the drawer and looked at the thing with the long handle and the deep round end, the thing you put into the soup to lift soup out of it, and I stood there holding it, and I said out loud, to the cat, who was not there, because it was not Thursday: “the soup spoon. The big one.”
I put it back in the drawer and closed the drawer and opened it again, the way you check a door you have just locked.
Still a soup spoon.

I sat on the kitchen floor. I am fifty-four. I had not sat on a kitchen floor since I was a child. I sat there with my back against the cupboard and I went through the drawer in my head, item by item, like a customs officer. Fork. Knife. Whisk. Grater. Corkscrew. Tin opener. Those were all there, each with its name on it, in four languages, neatly stacked. Only one was missing. One small label, gone.
I thought: tired. I thought: it is the rain. I thought: you are fifty-four and everyone forgets words at fifty-four and Inês forgot the word for fishmonger last month and laughed about it for a week.
But Inês had known the word was missing. She had felt the hole. She had said, oh, the man who sells the — the — what is it. She had gone looking.

I had not gone looking. Standing at the drawer, I had not felt a hole at all. The big soup spoon had seemed like a perfectly good name. It was only afterwards, on the floor, that I knew something was wrong, and I knew it the way you know there has been a step in the dark only when your foot comes down on nothing.

I will not bore you with the doctors. There were three of them, and a great many tests, and a machine I lay inside for forty minutes while it knocked and buzzed around my head like a woodpecker on a tin roof.
I will tell you about the pictures.

The neurologist was a young woman with very clean fingernails, at the big hospital on the hill, and she had a book of drawings. Simple black line drawings, the kind you would give to a child: a house, a chair, a clock, a pair of scissors. She turned the pages and I named them. It was easy. I am good at tests; I have always been good at tests. House. Chair. Clock. Scissors. Pen. Kettle. I was almost enjoying it.
Then she turned a page, and it was a drawing of a large bird standing in water on one leg, with a long neck folded like a letter S.
I said: “bird.”
She waited.

I said: “A water bird. A big one. Grey, I think, though of course it’s a drawing. They stand like that for a very long time and then they —” and I made a quick little stabbing movement with my hand, like a beak going into water.
She waited.
“I can’t,” I said.

She turned the page. A camel. I said camel at once, and I was so glad to have it that I said it twice. She turned the page. A rhinoceros. I said rhinoceros. She turned the page. A thing with a long body and many legs that lives under stones.
“Insect,” I said. And then, because I could hear how it sounded, I said: “Not an insect. More legs than that. You know. The ones under the — the stones.”
She wrote something down.

Afterwards she sat with me in a small room with a window onto a car park and a box of tissues on the table, which I took as a bad sign, since nobody puts out tissues for good news, and she told me what it was. She was very clear. I want to say that for her. She did not use long words to hide behind, the way doctors sometimes do; she used short ones, and she looked at me while she used them, and she told me the truth.

There is a part of the brain on the left side, under the temple, just in front of the ear, where the meanings of words are kept. Not the sounds of words. Not the grammar. The meanings — the thing that ties the sound heron to the grey bird standing on one leg. In me, she said, that part was very slowly wasting away. It had probably been happening for some time. It would go on happening. It was not the kind of forgetting most people fear at my age, where you lose your keys and your yesterdays. My memory of my life would most likely stay. I would remember the rain on the lake and the ceiling of Room Twenty and my mother’s face. I would still be able to speak, and speak well; my sentences would stay fluent, the grammar perfect, the tune of my voice the same. People who did not know me might not notice for a long while.

What would go was the meaning. One word at a time, the rarest first and the commonest last. Heron before bird. Ladle before spoon. Centipede — she said it gently, and I felt the name go into me like a key into the wrong lock — before insect. The specific things would turn into general things. The world, she said, would not go dark. It would go vague. It would lose its edges, and its names, and slowly the things in it would stop being anything in particular and become only thing.

It has a name, of course. Everything has a name except the things I need. It is called semantic dementia [suh-MAN-tik di-MEN-shuh], or, in the newer and longer version, the semantic variant of something called primary progressive aphasia [uh-FAY-zhuh]. Semantic, from the Greek, meaning to do with meaning. Aphasia, also Greek: without speech. Without speech, to do with meaning. I thought, sitting there, that the Greeks had been unusually exact.
I asked her how long.
She said it was different for everyone. She said many people live a long time with it, ten years, twelve. She said that was the wrong question.
I said what was the right question.
She said: “How long until you can’t do your job.”
I said: “And?”
She looked at me for a while, with her clean hands folded on the table.
“I think you know better than I do,” she said. “But I would guess a year. Perhaps less. In your work, the rare words are the work.”

The rare words are the work. I have thought about that sentence every day since. It is the truest thing anyone has said to me in a long time, and it was said by a woman of about thirty-two in a room that smelled of floor polish, while it rained on a car park.
I did what I always do before a difficult meeting. I read everything.

I read it in four languages, at night, at my kitchen table, with the window open onto the other balcony. Medical papers, which I could still follow then. Leaflets from charities in London and San Francisco. Forums where families write to each other at three in the morning. I want to put down here what I learned, in plain words, because the doctors’ words for it are long and Greek and they hide more than they show.
It is a kind of dementia. Most people, when they hear that word, think of the commonest kind, the one where a person forgets what happened yesterday, then last year, then who their children are.
Mine is a different kind, and much rarer. It does not start with memory. It starts with meaning. It eats the part of the brain where we keep what words and things are.

How rare? The families of illnesses it belongs to strike perhaps fifteen or twenty people in every hundred thousand in middle life, and mine is only one branch of that family, one in four or five of those. So: a few people in every hundred thousand. In a city the size of Geneva, perhaps a handful of us, walking about, saying the bird and the big spoon and hoping nobody notices.

It usually starts in the fifties or early sixties. I am on the early side. It almost never runs in families; for nearly everyone who has it, it simply arrives, for no reason anyone can find, like weather. There is no cure. There is no pill that slows it. There is only time, and how you spend it.

It begins on the left side of the brain, with words. Over the years it spreads across to the right side, and there it starts to take other things: the meaning of faces, so that people you love begin to look like strangers; the meaning of objects, so that a person can hold a fork and not know what it is for; and, often, parts of the personality itself. People become fixed in their habits. They want the same food at the same hour, every day. Some become very interested in clocks, or puzzles, or the colour yellow. Some lose the knack of feeling what other people feel, and become, without meaning to, unkind.

In the end, a person with it needs looking after all day and all night. Half of them live about twelve years or more after it begins; some much longer. When death comes, it usually comes from something ordinary, an infection in the chest, because the body has forgotten how to defend itself, as the mind forgot how to name things.

That is the plain account. It is accurate. It is also, like all plain accounts, missing the thing that matters, which is what it is like. For that I went to the people who had it, and the people who loved them.

The hospital runs a group on the first Thursday of every month, in a room with a coffee machine that has never once worked, for people with the language dementias and for the families who look after them. I went in April. I sat by the window. I did not take notes. I want to give you four of the people I heard there, with their names and small details changed.

A man of sixty-eight, who had set crosswords for a newspaper in Lausanne [loh-ZAN] for thirty years. That is the kind of joke this illness makes. He talked easily and well, with a big laugh, but every few sentences he would reach for a word and come back with a smaller one. The thing for the bread, he said, meaning the toaster. His wife sat beside him and said, quite matter-of-fact, that for a year now he would eat only food that was yellow: bananas, omelettes, a particular cheese. “He used to be the most adventurous eater I ever met,” she said. “Now if I put a tomato on his plate he looks at it as if I’d put a stone there.”

A woman of forty whose mother had the illness, seven years in. She said her mother still knew her voice on the telephone and would talk to her happily for an hour. But when she came to the door in person, her mother looked at her face and did not know it. “She knows me in the dark,” the daughter said. “She doesn’t know me in the light. So I’ve started ringing her from the car outside, before I go in, so she hears me first. It works about half the time.”

A man in his seventies who did not want to say much. He said only that his wife had been the kindest person he had ever known, and that the illness had taken her kindness before it took her words. That she now did the same thing at the same minute every day, and became frightened and angry if anything was moved, and no longer seemed to notice when he was sad. “I don’t blame her,” he said. “There’s no her left to blame. There’s just the illness, wearing her cardigan.”

And a woman of sixty-one, five years in, still working as a gardener in the parks. She said the Latin names of plants had gone first, the long ones she had been so proud of, then the French ones, then the ordinary words. Now she called nearly everything the green one or the one with the flowers. And then she laughed, a real laugh, and said: “But I still know which ones need water. My hands know. The names were never doing the watering.”
I came home from that room and sat on my kitchen floor, and I thought about the gardener for a long time. The names were never doing the watering. I wanted to believe her. I wanted it very much.
But I am not a gardener. In my work, the names are the watering. There is nothing else.
I did not tell anyone for three weeks. I went on working. I want you to understand how strange that was, and how easy.

It was easy because I am fluent. The doctor was right; my sentences did not falter. The words that were going were the rare ones, and in a meeting about a dam on a river, you can say the river a great many times before anyone needs a heron. When a hole opened in front of me, my mouth simply stepped around it, the way your feet step round a puddle without consulting you, and the meeting went on, and the red light glowed, and nobody downstairs in the ring of nations had the faintest idea that the English coming out of their earpieces was being made by a woman who was, very slowly, becoming vague.
It was strange because I could hear it.
Not the holes. I could not hear the holes; that is the cruelty of it. When the label is gone you do not feel the absence of the label. You feel nothing. You say the big spoon and it sounds fine.

What I could hear was the greyness. Listening back to myself in the evenings, on the recordings we are allowed to keep for training, I could hear the colour going out of my English. Where I used to say the delegate deplored, I said the delegate said he was unhappy. Where I used to say the wetland, I said the wet area. The marsh, even, which is a perfectly good word but not the word, the way a stone is a perfectly good thing to sit on but not a chair. It was all still correct. Nobody would have marked it wrong. It was simply that the sentences had started to look like the drawings in the doctor’s book. Clean black lines. A house. A chair. A bird.

For thirty-one years I had carried meaning across the dark in my cupped hands. Now I could feel it running out between my fingers, and the strangest thing — the thing I keep coming back to — is that it did not feel like loss. It felt like water finding its level. It felt almost restful. As though the world had been shouting at me in very precise terms all my life, and was now, kindly, lowering its voice.
That frightened me more than anything the doctor said.
I told Inês on a Thursday, in the booth, during the coffee break, with the microphones off.

Inês Barreto [ee-NESH ba-REH-too] is forty-one and comes from a small town in the north of Portugal where, she says, the only industries are saints and rain. She has worked beside me for nine years. In a booth you sit closer to your partner than to anyone else in your life — closer than a wife, closer than a priest — for seven hours a day, with your elbows touching, breathing the same small box of air, and you hear every swallow and every sigh and every time the other one gets something wrong and gets away with it. You cannot keep a secret from your partner for long. I had kept this one for three weeks and I think it was the longest she had ever known me to be quiet about anything.

She listened to the whole thing without interrupting, which is not like her. When I had finished she put her coffee down on the little shelf under the window and looked out at the ceiling of Room Twenty, all those coloured stalactites hanging over the empty ring of chairs.
“How many words,” she said.
“So far? I don’t know. That’s the point. I don’t know which ones are gone. I only find out when I reach for one.”
“Then we’ll keep a list,” said Inês.
That is Inês. Faced with the end of the world, she reaches for a pencil.

So we keep a list. It is in the back of my little black notebook, the one I use for difficult names before a meeting — the minister of this, the river that. At the top it says, in Inês’s handwriting, which is better than mine: Words gone. And under it, so far, there are eleven. I will not give you all of them. Some of them are embarrassing. One of them was nephew, and I have one.

But the first one on the list, at the top, in her careful hand, is heron. And underneath it, in brackets, because Inês is a translator to the bone and cannot bear a word on its own without its neighbours, she has written all the names it used to have: heron, héron [ay-RON], gém [GAME], čaplja [CHAP-lya].

I can read those. I can say every one of them aloud. They mean nothing to me. They are just sounds now, four small noises in four languages, like the croak a bird makes when it lifts off the water and is gone.
There is one more thing the doctor told me, and it is the thing that matters most, so I have left it for last.
I asked her what happens at the end. Not the end of the job. The end.

She did not pretend to misunderstand me. She said that in the later years people with this illness lose more than words. They stop knowing what a fork is for, not only what it is called. They stop knowing faces. They become, she said, choosing the word carefully, dependent. Many of them live a long time like that, peacefully, in rooms with soft chairs, looked after by kind people they cannot name.
Then she said something she was not obliged to say, and I have always been grateful to her for it.

“In this country,” she said, “you are allowed to choose not to get there. But you have to choose while you are still able to understand the choice. The law will not let anyone choose for you later. Not your family. Not a piece of paper you signed in advance. It has to be you, and you have to be clear when you do it. With your illness, that window does not stay open long.”
She did not say the name of the association. She did not need to. Everyone in Switzerland knows it. It is four letters long, written in capitals, and it means the way out.
I went home. I sat on the kitchen floor again; it was becoming a habit. And I understood, sitting there with my back against the cupboard, that I had been given two clocks, not one.
The first clock was the one the doctor had described: the slow one, the one that takes a word a week and turns the world from sharp to soft.

The second clock was quicker, and much colder. It was the clock that measured how long I would still have enough words to say, clearly, to a stranger with a form, I understand what I am asking for, and I am asking for it.
The rare words are the work, the doctor had said. I had thought she meant my job.

I took out my little black notebook, the one with the list in the back. I turned to a clean page. In my own handwriting, which is worse than Inês’s, I wrote down the words I would need to say at the end, in the language of the canton, so that I could practise them until I could say them in my sleep.
Je demande l’assistance. [zhuh duh-MAHND lah-sees-TAHNS] I am asking for help.
Then I wrote, underneath, in English, so that I could check later whether I still understood it:
This means: I want to die before I stop being able to say so.
I looked at that sentence for a long time. It was a good sentence. It was clean and plain and it said exactly one thing.
It was the first sentence I had written in thirty-one years that was entirely my own.
II. THE APPOINTMENT
Words gone this month: wren, gutter, verdict, mortgage, thimble, pillow, almond.
Let me tell you how it works, because almost nobody outside this country knows, and almost nobody inside it says it out loud.

In 1937, when Switzerland wrote down its criminal law, it put in a short paragraph about suicide. Article 115. It does not say that helping someone to die is allowed. It says something stranger and more Swiss than that. It says that a person who helps another to kill themselves for selfish reasons — to inherit the house, to be rid of the burden, to collect the insurance — can be sent to prison for up to five years.
That is all. It says nothing about the other kind.

For forty years nobody did much with that silence. Then, in the 1980s, a few people noticed what the paragraph did not say, and stood in the gap it left. If you help a person die without a selfish reason — because they asked you to, because they are suffering, because they have decided — then the law has nothing to say to you. You have committed no crime. A door had been standing open in the wall of the law since before the war, and nobody had walked through it.

They walked through it in 1982, here in Geneva. They called themselves EXIT, in capitals, which I have always thought was a very un-Swiss thing to do — to name yourself after a sign over a door in a cinema. Their full name is longer and politer: the Association for the Right to Die with Dignity. But everybody calls it EXIT. There is one in the German part of the country and one in the French part, and the French one is ours.

It is not a hospital. It is not a clinic, and nobody in it is paid to kill anyone. It is a club. You join it the way you join a library. You pay fifty francs a year. You receive a newsletter. Most of its members — and there are tens of thousands — never use it at all. They join the way you buy a fire extinguisher: to have it in the kitchen, and to sleep better knowing it is there.
If you do want to use it, there are rules, and the rules are the whole thing. I want to set them down plainly, because they matter for what comes after.

You must be eighteen. You must live in Switzerland. You must have an illness that cannot be cured, or suffering you find unbearable, or the many small failures of a very old body that add up to a life you no longer want. You must write a letter, by hand, asking for help. You must get doctors to write that you have this illness, and — this is the one that matters — that you have what the French call discernement [dee-sern-MAHN]. Discernment. The ability to understand what you are asking for, and what it means, and that it cannot be taken back.
And on the last day, you must do it yourself.

Nobody puts anything into you. A companion comes to your home — the association calls them accompagnateurs [a-kom-pan-ya-TUR], the ones who go along with you — and brings a small bottle of a powder called sodium pentobarbital [PEN-toh-BAR-bi-tal], fifteen grams, dissolved in water. It is roughly half a glass. It tastes, everyone says, very bitter. You drink it yourself, with your own hand, or, if your hands no longer work, you open the little tap on a drip yourself. You fall asleep within a few minutes. Most people are gone within half an hour, without waking.

Then the companion telephones the police. Because a death that is not natural must be investigated, the police come, usually two of them, with a doctor, and they ask the people in the room some questions and look at the papers, and they are, everyone says, very polite. Then they leave, and it is over, and it was legal, and it happened in your own bed.
That is how it works. A paragraph from 1937, a club, a letter, two doctors, a glass, and a quiet visit from the police.
I have interpreted treaties that were shorter and did less.
The rule that matters for me is the one about discernment, and I have to explain it carefully, because it is the cold heart of this whole book.

The doctors’ letter saying you can still understand your choice is only good for six months. After six months it must be written again. And every time it is written, a doctor must sit across from you and decide, honestly, whether you still understand.
For most people this is a formality. A man with a cancer that has reached his bones is as clear on his last day as on his first.

But for a person whose illness eats understanding itself — dementia, in all its kinds — the rule is a trap with a spring in it. The law will not let you decide in advance. You cannot sign a paper at fifty-four that says when I can no longer understand this paper, please help me. By the time you need the help, you are no longer the person who is allowed to ask for it. The door is only open while you can still read the sign above it. And the illness, by its nature, is the thing that is taking away your ability to read.

So people with dementia who choose this road must go early. Earlier than they want. Earlier than seems right. They must go while they are still well enough to be sure — which means while they are still well enough to have good days, and walks by the lake, and Thursdays with somebody’s cat. They must trade their good years for the certainty of not having the bad ones.

I did not know this before March. I learned it from a leaflet, and then from a woman with very clean fingernails, and then, most of all, from a man in a brown jacket in a room above a café, whom I will tell you about in a moment.

EXIT holds evenings. They are not secret, but they are not advertised either. Somebody who has been tells somebody who is thinking about it. Once a month, in a rented room in Plainpalais above a café that sells very bad croissants, about thirty people sit on folding chairs and a member of the association explains the rules, and then anyone who wants to may stand up and say why they came.

I went in April. I sat at the back, by the coat rack, the way I used to sit at the back of lecture halls when I was nineteen and new and afraid of being asked a question in French. I had my little black notebook on my knee. Old habit. When people talk, I take down the difficult words.

I want to give you some of what I heard, because I came to that room thinking I was the only person in the world with my particular problem, and I left understanding that I was just one more person standing at the same door. I have changed small details so no one can be recognised. I have not changed what they said.

There was a man of about seventy who had driven trams in this city for thirty-eight years. He had an illness that was slowly turning his muscles off, from the outside in. His hands were already weak; he held his coffee with both of them, like a child. He said: “The law says I must lift the glass myself. My hands are going. So I must go while my hands still work. I have perhaps six months of hands.” He said it the way you would say I have six months left on my lease. Then he said: “My wife wants me to wait. She says, one more summer. I want one more summer too. But if I wait for the summer I lose the glass.” He sat down. Nobody said anything for a while.
I wrote in my notebook: He has a hands clock. I have a words clock.

There was a very old woman, ninety-one, beautifully dressed, with a silk scarf and the posture of somebody who had once been a dancer, or a headmistress. She said she was not ill, exactly. She said: “Everything is a little bit broken and nothing is completely broken, and I am tired of being repaired.” She said: “I have buried my husband and my sister and my son. I have been to so many funerals I could run one. I do not want to be the last one at the party, washing the glasses.” People laughed, and she smiled, pleased that they had.

There was a younger woman, perhaps forty, who stood up and said she had not come for herself. Her mother had gone with EXIT the previous autumn. She said she had come to tell people what it was like on the day, because nobody had told her.

She said that it was a Tuesday. She said her mother had made her get up early to buy a particular kind of pastry from a particular bakery in Carouge [ka-ROOZH], because she wanted to taste it once more, and that her mother ate half of it and said it was not as good as she remembered, which made them both laugh. She said the companion was a retired schoolteacher with a grey plait who was so calm that she felt calm too. She said her mother drank the glass and made a face and said that is truly disgusting, and then she said well, I won’t have to taste it twice, and then she held her daughter’s hand and talked about a holiday in Brittany in 1989 when it rained every day, and then she was asleep, mid-sentence, and then about twenty minutes later she was gone.

She said the police came in two cars, very polite, and asked her where she had been standing and whether her mother had been sure, and she said yes, she has been sure for a year, she was the surest person I ever met. She said one of the police officers, a young man, took off his cap when he came into the bedroom, and that she would remember him for the rest of her life for doing that.

She said: “I thought it would be the worst day of my life. It was the second worst. The worst was the day the doctor told her what she had. The day she left was the day she got to choose.” She sat down. She was crying, and she was also, somehow, smiling, the way the old woman had smiled.
And then there was the man in the brown jacket.

He was sixty, perhaps. He did not stand up at first. He waited until everyone else had spoken and the woman running the evening was beginning to collect her papers, and then he stood, holding the back of the chair in front of him.

He said his wife had joined EXIT eight years ago, when she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. She had been a pharmacist. A very precise woman. She had known exactly what was coming. She had said to him, very clearly, more than once: when I don’t know you any more, I want to have gone.

He said they kept putting it off. One more Christmas. The wedding of a niece. A trip to Sicily they had always talked about. She was still herself, mostly. She still laughed at the right places. It seemed wrong to leave while it was still so nearly all right.

And then one spring the doctor sat across from her, as the rules require, and asked her the questions. And she got some of them wrong. Not many. Enough. And the doctor, who was a kind man, and an honest one, said he could no longer write that she understood.
The door closed. Just like that. Not with a bang. With a kind doctor looking sorry.

The man in the brown jacket said his wife was alive. He said she lived in a care home in Onex [oh-NAY], in a room with a soft chair, and that she was mostly peaceful. He said she did not know who he was. He said that sometimes she was frightened of him, because a strange man kept coming into her room and holding her hand, and that the nurses had asked him to visit less often.

He said: “I didn’t come here tonight to tell anybody what to do. I came to tell you one thing, because nobody told us. The door doesn’t stay open until you’re ready. The door stays open until it is ready to close. You think you’ll know when. You won’t. The illness doesn’t send you a letter.” He looked around the room at all of us on our folding chairs. “She wanted to go and I loved her too much to let her go early. That’s all. That’s what I did. I loved her too much and now she’s afraid of me.”
He sat down.

In my notebook, under He has a hands clock, I had written nothing. My pen had stopped. I sat in the back by the coats and I looked at that man’s brown jacket, at the shoulders of it, which were shaking very slightly, and I understood that I had just been told my future by the only person in the room who knew it.

I want to explain why I decided. Not the feeling of it — anybody can imagine the feeling. The reasons. I have spent my life believing that a thing is not understood until it can be said plainly, so I will try to say this plainly, and you can judge whether I have understood it.

The first reason is the simplest. I have no one to stay for. That sounds sadder than I mean it to. I have friends, and I have Inês, and I have my sister’s son in Szeged [SEH-ged], whose name I can still say even though the word for what he is to me has gone. But I have no child who would visit the soft-chair room and be frightened of. Nobody’s life would be shaped around my slow disappearing. If I stay, the only person the staying is for is me — and the doctor has told me, kindly, that the me it would be for will not be someone I would recognise.

The second reason is The Hague. For twenty years I carried the dead across the glass. Men and women and children who did not choose. Who were taken from their kitchens and their fields and their buses with no warning and no letter and no glass and no polite policemen taking off their caps. I said their deaths aloud eleven thousand times in a language that was not theirs. I do not say that I deserve a better death than they had. Nobody deserved what they had. I say only that, when I was offered a choice they were never offered, it seemed to me something close to rude to turn it down.
The third reason is the one that is hardest to say, and the one that matters most.

The doctor told me that, as the meanings go, the world does not go dark. It goes soft. Vague. Restful, even. And she was right. I have felt it already. When heron became bird, it did not hurt. When ladle became the big spoon, I did not grieve. A vague world is not a painful world. It is, if anything, a gentler one. Fewer edges. Less to carry.
That is what frightens me.

Because I think I could be happy there. I think the woman in the soft chair — the one who calls every bird bird and every spoon spoon and every face someone — might be perfectly content. She might sit by the window in Onex and watch the shapes go by and feel no lack at all. The doctor said it. The man in the brown jacket said it. Mostly peaceful.

And so the question I have had to answer is not do I want to suffer? I don’t think I will suffer much. The question is: does the woman I am now have the right to decide for the woman I will become? If she will be content, who am I to cancel her? She is me, after all. Or she will be.

I have turned this over every night since April, on the kitchen floor with my back against the cupboard, and this is the only answer I can find, and I give it to you plainly, for whatever it is worth.

She will not be me. She will be someone wearing my body and answering to my name — though she will not always know it is a name — and she will be, perhaps, at peace. But she will not be the person who carries meaning across the dark. She will not be the person who heard the delegate say le héron and knew in a quarter of a second exactly which grey bird on which leg in which shallow water he meant. That person — the one writing this — is made of exactly the thing the illness is taking. Not her memories, not her face. Her meanings. Take those away, a parcel at a time, and you do not get a quieter Margit. You get a house with all the labels peeled off every box, and someone living contentedly among the unlabelled boxes, who never knew what was in them, and never wonders.
I would rather close the house myself, while I can still read the labels.

That is my reason. I have tried to make it plain. I am not sure I have succeeded. It is the hardest thing I have ever interpreted, and the original is my own life, and I have no partner beside me to take over if I falter.
At the end of April I wrote the letter.
It must be written by hand. Not typed, not dictated. Your own hand, your own words. The association wants to see your hand doing it.

I sat at my kitchen table — not the floor; I thought the letter deserved a table — with a fountain pen I had not used in years, and a sheet of good paper, and I discovered something I had not expected.
I did not know how to write it.

I had written thousands of pages in my life. Every one of them was somebody else’s. A minister’s speech, carried into English. A witness’s testimony, carried into the record. Even my school essays, I realised, had been translations of what I thought the teacher wanted to hear. For thirty-one years I had been the most fluent woman in any room, and every word I had ever spoken in public had belonged to somebody else.
Now the association wanted one page of my own, and I sat at the table for two hours and could not begin it.

In the end I wrote it the only way I knew. I imagined that someone else was saying it — a woman of fifty-four, a stranger, sitting at a delegate’s desk in Room Twenty under the dripping ceiling — and I put her into French, half a breath behind her, as she spoke.

It took eleven minutes. It is the best interpreting I have ever done. I will not copy it here; it belongs to the association now, in a file. But I will tell you the last line, because I remember it, and because I think it is the truest thing in it.
Je voudrais partir pendant que je sais encore ce que veut dire partir. [zhuh voo-DRAY par-TEER pahn-DAHN kuh zhuh say ahn-KOR suh kuh vuh DEER par-TEER]
I would like to leave while I still know what leave means.
After the letter, the doctors. I will be brief, because doctors are brief.

The neurologist with the clean fingernails wrote the first certificate: the illness, its name, its course. She did not ask me why I wanted it. She only said, when she handed me the envelope, “You understand that for discernment I will have to see you again in six months, if you haven’t —” and she stopped, and chose another word, which I thought was a kindness, “— if you haven’t used it.”
I said I understood.
She said: “And you understand that with this illness, the next time, I may not be able to write it.”
I said I understood that too. I said it in four languages, as a joke, and she did not laugh, and I liked her for that.
The association’s own doctor — they call him the médecin-conseil [mayd-SAN kon-SAY], the advising doctor — read everything and agreed. Then the companion came to my flat.

She was not the schoolteacher with the grey plait. She was a retired nurse with a Fribourg [free-BOOR] accent and enormous, very gentle hands, and she sat on my sofa with a cup of tea for two hours and talked to me about everything except death — my work, my parents, the cat on Thursdays, the ceiling of Room Twenty, which she had seen once on television and thought looked like a cake left out in the rain. Only at the very end, putting on her coat, did she ask me, in the plainest possible French: “Are you sure?”
I said: yes.
She said: “You know you can change your mind at any moment. Even on the day. Even with the glass in your hand. Nobody will be disappointed. Nobody will think less of you. We will simply go home.”
I said I knew.
She said: “Then choose your day.”
My discernment certificate was dated the fourth of May. It would be good for six months: until the fourth of November.

The Human Rights Council’s autumn session ends in the second week of October. I have never in my career left a session unfinished, and I did not intend to start now. I would work the session to the last gavel. Then I would give myself two weeks, to clean the flat and give away the books and walk past the herons on the Rhône — the birds, I mean; the grey birds — one last time.

I chose a Thursday. The twenty-ninth of October. A Thursday, because the neighbour’s cat comes in on Thursdays, and I could say goodbye to him in the morning too, though he would not know it and would not, if I am honest about cats, much mind.
I wrote it in my little black notebook, in the front, where I write the dates of meetings. Thursday 29 October. 11:00. At home. It looked like an appointment with the dentist.
Then I closed the notebook and went to tell Inês.

I told her on a Monday, in the booth, at the end of the day, after the delegates had gone and the ceiling of Room Twenty was dimming, all those coloured points going grey one by one as the lights went down, like a forest at dusk.

She did not interrupt. She sat with her headphones round her neck and her hands in her lap and listened to the whole thing — the paragraph from 1937, the folding chairs, the man in the brown jacket, the letter, the date. When I had finished she did not say anything for so long that I thought she had not understood. Which would have been absurd. Inês understands everything. It is her gift. In our trade she is known, a little enviously, as the woman who can interpret the things that cannot be interpreted: the joke that only works in Portuguese, the prayer, the poem, the moment in a speech when a tired old diplomat stops reading his notes and says something true. Other interpreters go silent at those moments, or say the delegate makes a joke. Inês finds a way. Nobody knows how. I sat beside her for nine years and I do not know how.

When she finally spoke, she did not say don’t. She did not say are you sure, or have you thought, or what about the people who love you. I had prepared answers to all of those, and she said none of them.
She said: “The twenty-ninth.”
“Yes.”
“Thursday.”
“For the cat.”

She nodded slowly, as if that were the most reasonable thing in the world. Then she turned and looked at me properly, there in the half-dark of the booth, with the ceiling going out behind her, and I saw something in her face I had never seen in nine years of sitting at her elbow. Not grief. Not quite. Something more like a person standing at the top of a staircase in a dark house, deciding whether to tell you there is a room at the bottom you have never been in.
“Margit,” she said. “You’re going to the edge.”
“Yes.”
“Then you should look over it first.”
I said I did not know what she meant.

She was quiet again for a while. Then she said: “There’s something I’ve never told you. Something I’ve never told anyone. I’ve been trying to put it into words for nine years and I’ve never managed. Not in Portuguese, not in any of them.” She smiled, a strange, small smile. “You’re the only person I know who might be able to help me translate it.”

And then the cleaner came in to do the booths, and switched on the bright overhead light, and the moment broke, and Inês said, quite normally, “Come to my flat on Saturday. I’ll cook. I’ll tell you then.”

She stood up and put on her coat and left, and I sat alone in the booth for a long time under the bright light, with the dark ring of empty chairs below me, and my appointment in the front of my notebook, and her question in the back of my mind like a word just behind a door.
For the first time in months, I could hear something moving behind it.
III. THE SMELL OF BURNING PLASTIC
Words gone since May: sparrow, colander, sleeve, oath, lilac, tribunal, hinge, saucer, plum, ankle, envoy, rust, comma, crayon, kettle.

Inês lives in Carouge, across the river from the city, in an old part of town that was built by a king of Sardinia two hundred and fifty years ago to look like Italy. The streets are low and the houses are painted yellow and pink, and there are courtyards behind them with fig trees, and on a Saturday in May it smells of bread and wet stone.

Her flat is on the top floor, under the roof. It is full of plants and books and one enormous blue sofa that she says came up the stairs in 2015 and will only leave the same way when she does. She cooked fish with lemon and potatoes and we ate it at a small table by the window and talked about work, and I waited, and she waited, and neither of us said anything about anything until the plates were in the sink.
Then she went into her bedroom and came back with a cardboard box. The kind wine comes in. She put it on the table between us and took the lid off.
It was full of notebooks.

Cheap ones, school ones, the kind with soft covers and squared paper. There must have been twenty. Each one had a date on the front in black pen, and the dates ran from nine years ago until last month.
“I want you to read these,” she said, “and then I want to tell you what they’re about. Or the other way round. I’ve never been able to decide which order it goes in.”
I read them on the blue sofa until two in the morning, while she sat on the floor with her back against it and drank tea and did not interrupt me once.
I have to tell you what was in them, but I find it hard, for a reason you will understand in a moment.

Every page was an attempt to describe the same thing. One thing. A place, or a time, or an event; she was never sure which word to use, and neither, now, am I. She had tried it in Portuguese and in English and in French. She had tried it as a list. She had tried it as a poem. She had tried it as a letter to her mother, who had died before any of it happened. She had tried it as a set of instructions, as if for a traveller: turn left at the sound. She had drawn diagrams, and crossed them out. One notebook — the eleventh — was nothing but single sentences, hundreds of them, each on its own line, each starting with the words It was like.
It was like being inside a jewel that was also a song.
It was like walking into a room where everybody had been talking about you, kindly, and stopped, and cheered.
It was like the moment in a dream when you realise you can read, except the reading was the thing reading you.
It was like the day I was born, if I had been old enough to understand it, and they had been waiting with a cake.
It was like nothing. That is the problem. It was like nothing.

I read all of them. Some were beautiful. Some were funny. Some made the hair stand up on my arms. Inês is the best interpreter I have ever sat beside, and you could tell — every sentence was made by someone who knew exactly what words could do.

And every single one of them, I could see, had failed. Not because it was badly written. Because it was not it. She had written thousands of true sentences, and you could stack them as high as the Palais and they would not reach the thing they were pointing at. You could feel it on every page, the way you feel a cold draught under a door. There was a room on the other side of all those sentences, and not one of them had got her into it, and not one of them could get me in either.
At two in the morning I closed the twentieth notebook and put it back in the box.
“Well?” said Inês, from the floor.
I said: “Every sentence is true and none of them is it.”
She put her head back against the sofa cushion, beside my knee, and closed her eyes, and I heard her let out a breath she had been holding for nine years.
“Yes,” she said. “Yes. That’s it. That’s exactly it. Thank you.”
Then she told me.

Nine years ago her father died in Viana do Castelo [vee-AH-na doo kash-TEH-loo], the town of saints and rain. It was slow and it was hard. When it was over she went to stay with an old friend from interpreting school who lived in Porto, a woman she has not seen for years and will not name, and one night that friend gave her something to breathe in from a small glass pipe.

“She said it was the strangest thing in the world,” Inês said. “She said it would last about as long as it takes to boil an egg, and that I would not die, and that I would not be the same. She was right about all three.”

“And she said it would taste like burning plastic,” Inês added. “She was right about that too. Everybody says it. It’s the one thing everybody agrees on. Whatever happens after, it starts with the smell of a toy left on a stove.”
She did not tell me, that night, what she saw. She said: “You’ve read the notebooks. That’s as close as I can get. Closer, in a way, because now you know how far away it is.”
I asked her what it was. The thing in the glass pipe. What it was called.
She shook her head.
“No,” she said. “I’m not going to tell you that.”
I thought she was joking. She was not joking.

“If I tell you its name,” she said, “you’ll go home tonight and look it up. You’ll read everything. You’ll read it in four languages, the way you read everything, and by Tuesday you’ll know more about it than I do. And then if you go — if you go — you’ll go in carrying other people’s words. Theirs and mine. You’ll walk in with twenty notebooks under your arm.” She tapped the box. “I went in knowing nothing, Margit. Not even a name. It’s the only reason I have anything to write about at all.”
“That isn’t fair,” I said.

“No,” said Inês. “It’s the opposite of fair. You’ve spent thirty-one years carrying other people’s words into places. For once in your life, go in empty-handed.” She put the lid back on the box. “I’ll tell you its name when you come back. I promise. If you still want it.”

What she would tell me — what she insisted on telling me, there and then, before she would let me say another word — was the cost. I promised myself, when I began writing this, that I would not hide the cost of anything, so here it is, exactly as she gave it to me, without a name on it.

It is forbidden. Here, and almost everywhere else. To have it, or to give it, is a crime. In Portugal, where her friend had given it to her, taking a drug for yourself has not been a crime since 2001, only a matter for a sort of health committee — so that night in Porto, she had broken no law by breathing it in. Her friend, by handing it to her, had. And Inês had kept what was left — a little, in a small brown glass bottle at the back of her freezer — for nine years. In Geneva, she had been breaking the law every day of those nine years, and she was offering to break it again for me.

It is old. Older than any of the words for it. It grows, she said, in plants — in a great many plants, more than anyone has counted — and in the Amazon people have been brewing those plants into a bitter drink for longer than anyone has been writing things down. She would not tell me which plants. She said I would work it out, afterwards, and laugh.

It is strong. Nobody should take it lightly, or alone, or by surprise. For a short while you are not in the room at all. You cannot look after yourself. Someone sober must sit with you, and the room must be safe, and soft, and you must be lying down.
It can be terrifying. Not for everyone, not every time. But some people meet things there they do not want to meet, and come back shaking, and some of them do not sleep properly for weeks.

It is dangerous for some people’s minds and some people’s bodies. Anyone who has ever lost hold of what is real — or who has that in their family — must never take it; it can open a door in them that does not close. It makes the heart beat fast and hard for a few minutes; anyone with a weak heart must not. And it must never be mixed with certain medicines, especially some of the commonest pills for depression, because the two together can make the body’s own chemistry run wild, and that can kill.

I asked myself the questions. I have never lost hold of what is real; quite the opposite — I am losing hold of what things are called, not what they are. My heart, the doctors had told me, was the strongest thing about me. And when the neurologist offered me pills for my low mood in March, I had said no. I had wanted to feel all of it.

And it cannot be taken back. That was the last cost, and the one Inês was most careful about. “Most people come back glad,” she said. “Some come back frightened. Almost nobody comes back the same. You can’t unsee it, Margit. It isn’t a film. It goes in.”
I said: “In a year I won’t be able to see much of anything.”
She said: “That’s why.”

I did not decide that night. I want to be honest about that. I went home at three in the morning through the empty streets of Carouge and over the bridge, past the dark water where the grey birds stand in winter, and I sat on my kitchen floor, and I did not decide.

I did not decide in June, or in the long hot summer when the lake was full of swimmers and I lost the words for plum and lilac and ankle without noticing any of them go. Inês never asked. The brown bottle stayed at the back of her freezer. The appointment stayed in the front of my notebook.
I decided in October, in the last week of the autumn session, on a Tuesday, in the booth.

It was a debate about a war. Not a war I knew; a new one, far away, in a country I had never been to. A woman was speaking, a doctor who had worked in the hospitals there, and she was speaking in French, and I was carrying her into English, and she was describing what she had seen. And at one point she stopped, in the middle of a sentence, and the room went quiet, and she said, very simply, Je ne peux pas vous le dire. Il n’y a pas de mots. [zhuh nuh puh pah voo luh DEER. eel nyah pah duh MOH.]
I cannot tell you. There are no words.
And I said, into the microphone, half a breath behind her, perfectly calmly: “I cannot tell you. There are no words.”
And then she went on. And I went on.

But something in me had stopped and stayed stopped. Because I realised that I had said that sentence — there are no words — perhaps a thousand times in my life. Witnesses had said it to me at The Hague. Mothers. Doctors. Old men. There are no words for it. And every single time, I had carried it across the glass and set it down neatly in English, and never once in thirty-one years had I asked the obvious question.
Where is it, then? The thing there are no words for? Where does it go?

I was a woman who was losing her words one at a time. I had a little over three weeks before my appointment. And my friend had a small brown bottle at the back of her freezer, with no name on it, and twenty notebooks full of sentences that were all true and none of them it.

At half past eleven Inês touched my arm, and took over without a breath between us. I took off my headphones and leaned towards her and whispered, with the microphones off, under the ceiling of a thousand coloured points:
“Saturday. After the session.”

She did not stop interpreting. She did not even turn her head. But beside me, on the shelf under the glass, her left hand reached out and closed over mine, and held it, and went on holding it, all the way to the end of the doctor’s speech.
IV. THE DOME
Words gone since the summer: orchard, pebble, scarf, harbour, cousin, broom, ink, lantern, honey.

Saturday the tenth of October. The autumn session had ended the day before, at ten past six in the evening, with a gavel and a vote and a long round of thanks to the interpreters, which the delegates always give and never mean, and which we always accept and never believe. I took off my headphones for the last time that year and put them in the drawer under the window, and Inês put hers on top of mine, and we did not say anything.

That afternoon I walked to Carouge over the bridge. The grey birds were back on the river; there were two of them, standing in the shallows by the far bank, very still. I stopped and looked at them for a while. I knew everything about them except what to call them. It no longer frightened me. It was simply a fact, like the weather.

I am going to tell you what happened next in seconds, because that is the only honest way to tell it. Inês sat beside me with her watch, and afterwards she wrote down the times for me, and I have checked them against everything I remember, and they are right. It was very short. You will not believe how short. I did not believe it either.
Second 0.

The blue sofa. Cushions under my head and under my knees. Inês had drawn the curtains half closed, so the room was the colour of weak tea. A candle — the small light with the flame, I mean; the word has gone since — on the table. A glass of water I would not need. A blanket.
She had shown me how to hold the thing: a small glass pipe, no longer than a pencil. She lit it for me, and told me to breathe in slowly, and hold it, and breathe in again.

The first breath tasted of nothing I knew. Then of something I did: burning plastic. A child’s colouring stick of wax — that word has gone too — held in a flame. Something chemical and sweetish and wrong, like a toy left too near a fire.
I held it in. I breathed out.
Second 8.
The second breath. Already the room was louder. Not the sounds in it; the room itself. As if the walls had turned up their own volume.
Inês’s voice, from very close, saying: “Once more. If you can.”
Second 15.

The third breath. I did not finish it. Inês took the pipe out of my fingers. I remember thinking, very clearly, very calmly, in English: she has taken it, so I do not drop it. It was the last ordinary sentence I had for some time.
And then the sound.
I have to describe the sound carefully, because everyone who has been where I went describes the same sound, and I did not know that then.

It was like someone crumpling a sheet of cellophane right beside my ear. Or the thin paper bag the bread comes in, being screwed up in a fist. A dry, bright, crackling sound, getting louder, close, inside my head and outside it at once. And under it — no, through it — a sense of something being torn. Not violently. Carefully. As if someone were tearing a very thin skin, a membrane, slowly, from one end to the other, so that something on the other side could get through. Or so that I could.
And a hum. Rising. The kind of hum a machine makes before it starts.
Second 22.
Colour.
Every colour in the room got brighter all at once, as if someone had wiped a dirty window. The weak-tea light went gold. The blue of the sofa went so blue it hurt, a blue that was almost a sound.
Then, in front of my eyes — not in the room; in front of the room, as if painted on the inside of my eyelids, though my eyes were open — something began to turn.

It was a flower. Or something like a flower. Round, made of many layers of petals, red and orange, and it was turning, slowly, the way a wheel turns, and every petal was made of smaller petals, and every one of those was turning too. It was very beautiful and very regular and it was getting bigger, or I was getting closer to it, and I understood without being told that it was a kind of door. A round door made of turning red and orange. And that the tearing sound and the turning flower were the same thing, seen and heard.
I remember thinking: I don’t have a word for this.
And then, quite clearly, with something almost like a laugh: nobody does.
Second 40.
I went through.

I don’t know how else to say it. The flower opened, or I did, and there was a feeling — the only word I have is rupture — of something giving way completely, all at once, the way ice gives way. And I was not on the sofa. I was not in Carouge. I was not anywhere that has a name.
I was inside.
Second 41.
Here is where I must be very careful, and very plain. Everything I say now is wrong. But some of it is less wrong than the rest, and that is the best any of us can do.

I was in a room. A round room, with a high, curved roof, like the inside of a dome. Like the inside of an egg, if the egg were the size of a church. It felt as if it were underground, or deep inside something, and yet it was full of light — a warm, steady, golden light that came from everywhere at once, from the walls, from the air.

The walls were moving. Not shaking; working. They were covered in patterns, and the patterns were alive, folding and unfolding, flowing into new shapes so quickly and so perfectly that it was like watching a thousand hands do a thousand card tricks at once. Every pattern was perfect. Every pattern became another perfect pattern. Nothing was still, and nothing was chaos. It was the opposite of chaos. It was more orderly than anything I have ever seen, so orderly it seemed to be thinking.
And it was safe. That surprised me most. It felt like the safest place I had ever been. Like the room you are born into, if you could remember it. Warm and lit and expecting you.
That was when I noticed I was not alone.
Second 44.
They came all at once, from everywhere, and the first thing they did was cheer.

I have to say that plainly, because it is the strangest part and I will not make it sound more dignified than it was. They cheered. A great, high, happy noise, like a crowd of children when the birthday cake comes through the door. A sort of hhheeyyyy, rising, delighted. She’s here. She’s here. She’s come.

They were small, or seemed small. They were made of light, or of something hard and bright, like jewels, like polished glass and metal and pearl. They did not keep one shape. Each of them was changing all the time — folding, opening, turning inside out and back again — the way the patterns on the walls were changing, but faster, and with more joy in it. They bounced. They tumbled over each other. They were like bright little machines that had learned to be glad, or like gladness that had learned to be a machine.

I knew what they were. I don’t mean I knew their name. I mean I knew, the way you know a friend’s step on the stairs before you see them, what kind of thing they were. They were the ones who live here. And they had been waiting for me. Not for someone. For me. They knew me.

Later, when I came back, I would learn that a man had given them a name, long before I ever heard of him, and that the name was elves. I laughed when I heard it. It is a silly word. It is also, I have to admit, the right one.
Second 60.
One of them came very close. Right up to my face, if I had a face there, which I am not sure I did.
And it said — not in words; I will come to how it said things — something I understood perfectly. It said: Don’t give way to amazement.
Not unkindly. The way a teacher says it to a child who is staring with her mouth open at the blackboard instead of reading what is written on it. Don’t stand there gaping. Look. Pay attention.
I did not know how much time I had. I knew, somehow, that it was not much. And I understood that amazement was a waste of it. That the place was not for being amazed in. It was for paying attention.
So I paid attention. I am an interpreter. Paying attention is the only thing I have ever been good at.
Second 90.
They were singing.
I want to say that more exactly, because it matters more than anything else that happened, and because it is the thing I was there to see, though I did not know it.
They were singing, and their singing was not about things. Their singing made things.

When one of them sang, the song came out of it not as a sound but as an object. A shape. You could see it. It hung in the golden air in front of you: a small, perfect thing, like an egg made of glass and light, turning slowly, covered in patterns, glowing from inside. And you understood it. Not by translating it. By looking at it. Its meaning was not attached to it the way a label is attached to a parcel. Its meaning was it. The shape and the meaning were the same thing.

That is the nearest I can come. In our world, a word is a sound that points at a thing. Heron points at the grey bird. The sound and the bird are different things, tied together by a thread, and the thread can break — as mine have been breaking, one by one, since March. But there, in the dome, there was no thread. There was no gap between the word and the thing. The word was the thing. You did not say bird and hope someone pictured the bird. You sang, and there was the bird, made of song, and anyone could see it, in any language, or in none.
They were showing me language you could see.

And I, who had spent thirty-one years carrying meanings across the gap between words and things, half a breath behind other people, with my cupped hands, terrified of spilling — I understood, watching them, that there is a place where there is no gap at all. Where nothing needs carrying, because nothing is ever apart from what it means.
I think that was when I started to cry. Inês tells me I did. I don’t remember the crying. I remember the eggs of light.
Second 200.
Then they showed me what they had brought.
It is hard to say how long I had been there. Inês’s watch says a little over three minutes. It felt like an afternoon. It felt like a life.

They gathered in front of me, all of them, bouncing, delighted, the way children gather when they have made you a present and cannot wait for you to open it. And they sang, together, one long song, and out of their song a shape grew in the golden air.

It was long and grey. It stood on one leg in a pool of something that was not water but behaved like water. Its neck was folded like a letter S. It was made of light and glass and patience. It was utterly still. And then — it struck, a quick bright movement, like a beak into water — and then it was still again.
I knew it at once.
It was the bird. My bird. The grey one from the river. The one I lost in March, in the booth above Room Twenty, when the delegate said le héron and I said the animal.

And I could see its name. Not hear it; see it. The name was not a sound tied to the bird with a thread; the name was the bird itself, the whole shape and stillness and strike of it, and I could see it, and I could read it, and I knew what it meant more completely than I had ever known any word in my life.
The elves cheered. You see? You see? It’s here. We’ve got it. It’s safe.
Second 260.
Then they showed me the next one.
A long-handled thing with a deep round end, made of silver light, dipping into something warm and lifting it out. My big spoon. My ladle. Here, with its meaning on it, whole.
And then a small brown bird, very round, with its tail cocked up, singing a song too loud for its size: the wren.

And then a thing I had never seen with my eyes but knew instantly: the word for a promise to pay back a house over thirty years, which had gone from me in April, standing in the air like a small heavy building made of patience and worry.

And then the word for my sister’s son. Not his name; I still had his name. The word for what he is to me. It came as a shape I cannot describe except to say that it was warm, and familiar, and looked a little like my sister, and a little like me, and it was so plainly what it was that I laughed out loud, there in the dome, and the elves laughed with me.

And then more. And more. Faster now. Every word on Inês’s list. The almond, the hinge, the saucer, the plum. The sleeve, the comma, the kettle. The lilac. The orchard, the lantern, the honey. Each one sung into the air in front of me, whole, perfect, glowing, with its meaning not tied to it but being it. Each one greeted with a cheer. A whole procession of them, like a parade, like the end of a long war when the soldiers come home and the crowd goes mad on the pavements.
That is what I understood, watching them come.
They were not lost.

I had thought, since March, that my words were being destroyed. Rubbed out. Wiped off the inside of my head like chalk off a board. That each one was a small death. That I was dying, very slowly, one word at a time.

But they were here. Every one. Not destroyed. Gone ahead. Gone home, or gone back, or gone to wherever words come from in the first place, before anyone ties them to a sound. And the ones who lived here had been collecting them. Keeping them. Waiting, with tremendous excitement, for me to arrive and see them all again.
Second 400.
And then the elves did something I did not expect.

They stopped singing my words. They went quiet — or as quiet as they ever were, which was still a sort of busy, delighted fizz — and they drew back, and made a space in front of me. And into that space, slowly, something came that was not one of my words at all.

It was bigger than the others. It was not clear and bright like them. It was dark at the edges and very dense, like a stone, or a storm cloud, or the inside of a fist. And it was made of many things pressed together, too many to count. I looked into it, and I saw — I don’t know how to say this — I saw faces. Hands. A kitchen. A bus at a roadside. A field. A woman’s voice, in my father’s language, stopping in the middle of a sentence.
I knew what it was.
It was everything there had been no words for.

Every time, in thirty-one years, that someone in front of me — a witness, a doctor, a mother, an old man — had stopped and said, I cannot tell you. There are no words. Every one of those things they could not say. I had carried the sentence there are no words across the glass a thousand times, and never once asked where the thing itself went, the thing there were no words for.
It came here.

It was all here. Kept. Not forgotten. Not wiped away. The elves had kept it too, with the same care they kept my heron and my ladle. It was heavy, and dark, and terrible to look at, and they held it up to me with the same gentleness they had held up the wren, as if to say: This too. This is ours too. Nothing is lost here. Not the small words and not the things too big for words. We keep all of it.
I wanted to look away. One of them came close to me again, and I understood it to say, very gently, the thing it had said before.
Don’t give way to amazement. Pay attention.
So I looked.

I will not tell you what I saw. Not because I won’t. Because I can’t. Not yet. Some of what I carried back I have had to carry the way I carried everything else in my life: one word at a time, carefully, with my hands cupped. I will try, later. I promise you I will try.
Second 600.
Then it began to fold away.

Not suddenly. Kindly. The way the end of a good evening folds away, people standing up and finding their coats and kissing each other at the door. The golden light was still there but further off. The patterns on the walls were slowing. The elves were still bouncing, still glad, but they were waving now — I don’t know with what; they had no hands, they had everything — and I understood that they were saying goodbye, and also, at the same time, something that was the opposite of goodbye.
See you soon.
Not see you again. See you soon. As if they knew something about my calendar that I had been trying not to know.

And then one more. One last word, sung into the air in front of me, very small, very bright, and I did not recognise it. It was not one of mine. Not yet. It was a word I still had. I could feel it, still tied to its sound, still sitting in my head where it belonged.
They showed it to me anyway. As if to say: this one’s coming too. Not yet. But it’s coming. We’ll keep it for you.
I am not going to tell you which word it was. It is still mine, for now. When it goes, I will know where.
Second 740.
The ceiling of Inês’s flat. Cracked plaster. A stain the shape of Italy. The weak-tea light through the half-closed curtains.
