The candle — the small light — still burning on the table. A blanket over my knees that I did not remember. My face wet. My hands, both of them, held in both of Inês’s.

I tried to speak and found that I could. My mouth worked. My English was there. My French. My Hungarian. My father’s language. All the ordinary words, the common ones, the ones the doctor said would go last, sitting in my head as if nothing had happened, waiting patiently to be used.
I turned my head and looked at Inês. She was crying too. She had a notebook open on her knee — the twenty-first notebook; I learned that later — and her pen was still in her hand.
She said: “Welcome back.”
And I said the only thing I could say. The plainest sentence I had. I said it in English, because it is the language I have been paid to tell the truth in for thirty-one years.
I said: “They kept them. Inês. They kept every one.”
V. THE TWENTY-FIRST NOTEBOOK
Words gone since the dome: candle, ferry, glove, quarry, vinegar, chimney.

I slept on the blue sofa that night. I did not mean to. I meant to drink the water, and say thank you, and walk home over the bridge in the dark like a grown woman. Instead I lay with the blanket over my knees and looked at the stain on the ceiling that was shaped like Italy, and the next thing I knew it was Sunday, and the light was white, and Inês was making coffee in the kitchen and singing very quietly in Portuguese.
She brought me a cup and sat on the floor with her back against the sofa, the way she had sat the night I read her notebooks, in May.
“You promised,” I said.
“I did.”
“You said you would tell me its name. When I came back. If I still wanted it.”
“Do you?”

I thought about it. I want to be honest: I really did think about it. For a moment I wanted to leave it without a name forever. To keep it the way they had kept my words, whole, with nothing tied to it.
But I am an interpreter. I have never in my life been able to leave a thing without its name.
“Yes,” I said.
She told me.
It is called dimethyltryptamine [dye-METH-il-TRIP-tuh-meen]. It is a long word, and nobody uses it. Everybody says the three letters at the front of it instead.
DMT.

I said it out loud, once, to try it. Three letters. Three small sounds, tied by a thread to the dome, and the gold, and the elves, and the turning red-orange door. I could feel the thread as I said it. I could feel how thin it was. I laughed, because it was so much smaller than the thing, and Inês laughed too, because she had laughed the same laugh nine years ago, in Porto, on a different floor.
“Now,” she said. “Now you can read everything.”

So I did. I want to tell you what I learned, plainly, in the order I learned it, the way I would give a delegate the background to a resolution before the vote. I went home that Sunday and sat at my kitchen table with the books and the papers and a dictionary beside me for the words I no longer have, and I read for two days.
I will make it as simple as I can. I find that is easier for me now than it used to be. You will see why.

DMT is a very small thing. A molecule [MOL-uh-kyool]. A molecule is just a shape made of atoms stuck together, far too small to see. This one is made mostly of carbon and hydrogen, with a little nitrogen.

It is a close relative of something your brain already uses every second of your life. That thing is called serotonin [seh-roh-TOH-nin]. Serotonin is one of the brain’s messengers. It carries signals from one brain cell to the next, and it helps to set your mood, and your sleep, and the way the world looks to you when you open your eyes in the morning.

The two shapes are so alike that DMT fits into some of the same locks in the brain that serotonin fits into. One lock above all. The scientists call it by a code: 5-HT2A [five-aitch-tee-two-AY]. When DMT turns that lock, the brain’s ordinary way of building the world — this is a room, this is a sofa, this is me, that is you — comes apart. Not for long. But completely.
That is what it does. Nobody yet knows why it does that, and not something else. Nobody knows why, when the ordinary world comes apart, so many people find the same other world underneath it.
Here is the first thing that made me laugh, the way Inês said I would.
She had told me it grew in plants, a great many plants, more than anyone had counted. She would not tell me which. She said I would work it out afterwards, and laugh.

She was right about the plants. It is in hundreds of them. It is in the leaves of a shrub in the Amazon. It is in the root bark of a tree in the dry northeast of Brazil, which the people there call jurema [zhoo-REH-ma]. It is in certain grasses, and in the bark of certain acacias, and in some of the reeds that grow at the edge of lakes. Perhaps, for all I know, at the edge of ours.
But here is why I laughed. It is in us.

Small amounts of it have been found in human blood, and in the clear fluid that the brain floats in. In 2019 a group of scientists found that the brains of rats make it, quite ordinarily, in amounts close to some of the brain’s other messengers. Nobody knows what it is doing there. There are many guesses. Not one of them is proven.
It is simply there. A key the body seems to cut for itself, to a door nobody has found.

I had gone to Carouge with my coat and my umbrella, thinking that I was going to be given something strange from far away. And all that time the strange thing had been at home. In the plants by the river where the grey birds stand. In me.
Here is the second thing. If you swallow it, nothing happens at all.

The stomach has a cleaner in it, an enzyme [EN-zime], whose job is to break things like this down before they can get any further. It breaks DMT down almost at once. You could eat a plate of those Amazon leaves and feel nothing but full.

The people of the Amazon found a way round that cleaner a very long time ago — longer ago than anyone has written down. They boil the leaf together with a second plant, a thick woody vine, and something in the vine stops the cleaner from working. That is the bitter brown drink Inês had told me about in May. It is called ayahuasca [eye-uh-WAHS-kuh]. It lasts for hours, not minutes, and people who drink it are often very sick before they are anything else. It is a story for another book.

If you breathe DMT in, as smoke or as vapour, it goes past the stomach altogether, straight into the blood, and up into the brain in ten or fifteen seconds. That was the third breath; that was the cellophane, and the tearing, and the hum. And most of it is gone again in about twelve minutes.
Inês’s friend in Porto had been exact. As long as it takes to boil an egg.

And the burning plastic is real, too. It is the taste of the thing itself, warmed in glass. Everyone who has ever breathed it says the same. It is the only part of the whole journey that everybody agrees how to describe.
I find that funny. The one thing in the world we all have the same words for is the smell of the doorstep.
Here is the history. In order, and short.
In 1931, a chemist in Canada named Richard Manske made it for the first time, in a laboratory, out of other chemicals. He wrote it down. He did not try it. Nobody tried it for twenty-five years.
In 1946, a scientist in Brazil found it growing in nature, in the root of the jurema tree.

And in 1956 — this is the part I read three times — in Budapest, in my city, in the year of the uprising, fifteen years before I was born there, a young Hungarian doctor and chemist named Stephen Szára [SAH-rah] wanted to study the mind.

He wanted to use LSD, the famous new drug that a company in Basel, here in Switzerland, had begun to make. He wrote to them and asked if he could buy some. They said no. They did not want, they said, such a powerful thing going into a communist country.

So Szára, who was a chemist before he was a doctor, made DMT himself, in his own laboratory. He tested it on rats. He tried swallowing it, and nothing happened, which you now know is the stomach’s cleaner at work. And then, one day in April 1956, he injected it into a muscle, to see what would happen.
He wrote that his mind was filled completely with visions, and that he felt an intense, overflowing joy. He said afterwards that some of that joy was simply the joy of having found something.

Afterwards he gave it to colleagues who offered themselves, carefully, and wrote down what they told him. Not all of them were glad. One said it was too much. Another, a doctor, called it a dangerous game, and said it would be easy not to come back from it.

That autumn, the Soviet tanks came into Budapest. My mother was nine years old. She told me, when I was a child, about the sound of them on the cobbles at night, and about the windows of the bakery on her street, and about the neighbours who were there one week and gone the next. Two hundred thousand people left Hungary that winter, over the border into Austria, through the snow and the marshes, carrying what they could. Stephen Szára left too, soon after. He went to America and spent the rest of his long life studying the brain, in the government’s own laboratories near Washington. He died in 2021, at ninety-eight.
He never lived in Budapest again.

I sat at my kitchen table with this in front of me and thought: he was the first person we know of to walk through that door on purpose and come back and say what was there. He did it in my city. He did it in the same year my mother listened to the tanks. And then he left, and carried what he had seen out of the country, the way the others carried their children and their candlesticks. And never once set it down in the place it came from.

I am not superstitious. I have sat in rooms with too many men who were sure that God or history was on their side to believe in signs. But I am an interpreter, and I know what it is to carry something out of one place and set it down in another, carefully, with your hands cupped. I felt — I will say it plainly — that I had been handed something by a stranger from my own street, seventy years late.
After Szára, others.

In the early 1990s an American psychiatrist named Rick Strassman, at a university in New Mexico, gave DMT to about sixty volunteers, slowly and carefully, in a hospital research ward, with a nurse beside them, and wrote down everything they told him. He called it the spirit molecule. He was a careful man and did not expect what he heard.
What he heard, over and over, from people who had never met each other, was this: there was someone there.

Not always the same someone. Some of the volunteers met beings who were gentle, and some met beings who were busy and paid them no attention, like workers in a factory, and some met beings who frightened them. Some were like insects, some like clowns, some like light. But they were there. They seemed to have been there before the volunteers arrived, and to be going on with their own lives after they left. And very often, they seemed to know the volunteers were coming.

Then, in 2018, a group of scientists at Imperial College in London did something simple and very clever. They gave DMT to volunteers, and when the volunteers came back, they asked them the same list of questions that doctors ask people who have nearly died. People whose hearts have stopped on an operating table. People who have drowned and been pulled out and breathed back into.

The answers were very close. Closer than the scientists had expected. Leaving the body. A tunnel, or a door. A light. A feeling of arriving somewhere more real than here, not less. Meeting someone who seemed to be waiting. Being sent back.
I read that in my kitchen on the Monday afternoon and I put the paper down and thought of the elves waving, and of the thing they said that was the opposite of goodbye.
See you soon.
And it is forbidden. I promised myself I would not hide the cost of anything, so here it is again, now with its name on it.

In Switzerland, DMT is on the list of forbidden drugs. To have it is a crime. To give it is a worse one. The same is true almost everywhere on earth. Since 1971 an agreement between nations, signed by nearly every country there is, has put pure DMT in its strictest class, on the same shelf as LSD and mescaline.
There are only a few gaps in that wall, and they are strange ones.

The agreement forbids the pure substance. It does not forbid the plants it grows in. So in Brazil and in Peru, the old Amazon drink is legal, and in Brazil it is drunk openly, in churches, on Sunday, with hymns. In the United States, two of those Brazilian churches went to court for the right to drink it in their ceremonies, and won; in 2006 the highest court in that country agreed with the first of them, without one voice against. In 2022 the people of one American state, Colorado, voted that a grown adult should no longer be punished for taking it, though selling it is still a crime there, and the national law still calls it one everywhere else.

And in Portugal, since 2001, taking any drug at all for yourself has not been a crime. Only a matter for a kind of health committee, who may talk to you, and may send you to someone who can help. Giving it to another person is still a crime. So that night in Porto, nine years ago, Inês broke no law at all. Her friend, by handing her the pipe, did.

And Inês, by keeping the little brown bottle at the back of her freezer for nine years, in Geneva, broke the law of this country every single day. And by holding the pipe to my mouth on a Saturday afternoon, she broke it again, worse, for me.
Nowhere on earth can you walk into a shop and buy pure DMT. Not legally. Not anywhere.
There. Now you have everything I have. The name, and the cost, and the history, and the law.
None of it is what happened to me. All of it is true, and none of it is it.
The last name I learned that week was the one I had heard already, without knowing it.

His name was Terence McKenna. He was an American, born in 1946 in a small town in Colorado, among cattle ranches and mountains. He breathed DMT for the first time in 1965, as a young man in California, and many times after that. And he spent the rest of his life trying to say what was there.

Not in a laboratory. Not in a hospital, with a nurse and a list of questions. In public. On stages, in halls, on the radio, on cassette tapes passed from hand to hand. In ordinary words. With jokes. He would stand up in front of a room of strangers and tell them, as calmly as if he were describing a trip to the shops, that he had breathed in a chemical and gone through a door and been greeted by a crowd of small, delighted, jewel-like creatures who were made of something like light and something like machines, and who changed shape as he watched, and who sang things into the air that you could see.
He was the one who gave them their name. He called them self-transforming machine elves. He knew it was a ridiculous name. He used it anyway, because it was the nearest he could get.

He said they cheered when he arrived. He said they rushed at him like children. He said their singing was a kind of language that did not need to be heard, because it could be looked at — that the words were not pointing at things; they were the things. He said one of the beings had told him, in effect: don’t stand there gaping; don’t give way to amazement; look. And he spent thirty-five years telling the world that the strangest part was not the strangeness. The strangest part was that it seemed to be there, whether he came or not, and that it seemed to know him.
I read that, at my kitchen table, and I had to get up and walk to the window and stand there with my hand over my mouth.

Because I had not read it before. I had gone in empty-handed, the way Inês made me. I had never heard his name. I had never heard the word elves, not in that sense. Not one sentence of his had been in my head on the blue sofa.

And he had seen what I had seen. Forty, fifty, sixty years before me. In another country, in another language, with a completely different life behind him. The cheering. The jewels. The singing you could see. Don’t give way to amazement. The very words.

I want to be careful here. I am not telling you that this proves anything. Inês had read him, years ago, after Porto; perhaps something she said, once, in a booth, in a café, slipped into me without my noticing. Perhaps all of us who go through that door are only meeting the shape of our own brains, and our brains are all built from the same plan, so of course we meet the same things. That is possible. I have sat in enough courtrooms to know that ten honest witnesses can all describe the same thing that was never there.
But I have also sat in enough courtrooms to know what it sounds like when ten honest witnesses describe the same thing that was.
McKenna died in the year 2000. He was fifty-three. He died of a tumour in his brain.
I sat with that for a long time, too.
On the Tuesday evening, Inês came to my flat with a bottle of wine and the twenty-first notebook.
She put the notebook on the kitchen table, between us, the way she had put the wine box full of the other twenty on her own table in May. She did not open it. She put her hand flat on the cover.
“I need to tell you something first,” she said, “and then you can read it, and then you can tell me I’m mad.”
I waited.
“You talked,” she said. “The whole time. From about the fiftieth second until about the tenth minute. You talked without stopping.”
I said I didn’t remember talking. I remembered the elves talking. I remembered the eggs of light.

“I know,” said Inês. “It wasn’t any language. Not one I know, and I know seven, and I can recognise the music of twenty more. It wasn’t French or Hungarian or your father’s language. It wasn’t nonsense, either — not babbling. It had sentences. It had a shape. It went up at the ends of things and down at the beginnings. It had stops in it, like breathing, where the sense finished and started again. It sounded —” she stopped, and I watched her look for the word, and find it, and not like it, and use it anyway. “It sounded like the most fluent thing I have ever heard. More fluent than you in the booth on your best day. It sounded like somebody who has never once in her life had to look for a word.”
“And you wrote it down,” I said.
“No,” said Inês. “That’s the thing. I didn’t write it down. I couldn’t have. There’s no alphabet for it.” She took her hand off the notebook. “I interpreted it.”
“Into what?”

“Into English. Live. Half a breath behind you. The way we do.” She looked at me, and I saw that she was frightened, which I had never seen in nine years. “I didn’t decide to. I had the pen in my hand to write down the times, and you started talking, and I just — went. The way you go in the booth when the delegate starts and the red light comes on. I didn’t think about it. My hand did it. I couldn’t have stopped it if I’d wanted to.” She pushed the notebook across the table to me. “I haven’t read it back properly. I couldn’t. I wanted you to be the first.”
I opened it.
I am going to give you some of what she wrote. Not all of it. Some of it is mine, and some of it I am still carrying.

You have heard me say, over and over, that I am good at plain words, and that plain words are all I have left. Inês is not like me. She never was. She is the one who can describe the thing nobody has seen. She is the one who, in the booth, when a delegate stumbles into a sentence with no bottom to it, can somehow give it one. Nine years she had spent failing to describe her own journey, in twenty notebooks, because she had been inside it. This time she was outside. She was sitting beside the door, watching me go through, and listening to me sing from the other side of it, and carrying it across.
This is what she wrote. The times in the margin are hers.
0:50 — She has begun to speak. Her eyes are open and not here. Her voice is low and quick and certain, the voice of a woman giving directions in a city she was born in.
Here is the room. It was always here. It is under the floor of every room. You walk across it all your life and you hear it sometimes in the boards when the house is quiet.
1:15 — They are glad. Tell them I am glad also. No — tell them I am the gladness. They will understand that better.

1:40 — Look how they make the words. Look. They open their mouths and the thing comes out whole, like a fish from the water, wet and shining and alive, and you do not have to ask what it is. It tells you, by being it. Nobody here has ever needed an interpreter. Nobody here has ever been lonely in a sentence.
2:10 — Her hands are lifting off the blanket, as if to catch something thrown. She is laughing. I have never heard her laugh like this. It is the laugh of a girl.
2:30 — Oh, they say. Oh, you came. We have been keeping your things.
3:20 — Here she said one word, a single word, three times, slowly, as if teaching it to me. It was not a word. It was not in any language. And my hand wrote — heron. heron. heron.
3:40 — A long tall shape of patience standing in a river of light. It strikes. It is still again. It is still a bird. It was always a bird. It is only the string that broke.

4:00 — and then my hand wrote, faster than I could think, one after another: ladle — centipede — nephew — wren — gutter — verdict — mortgage — thimble — pillow — almond — sparrow — colander — sleeve — oath — lilac — tribunal — hinge — saucer — plum —
— and on, and on, down the page, faster than I could keep up —
— kettle — orchard — pebble — scarf — harbour — cousin — broom — ink — lantern — honey —
— candle.
She is saying each one as if it is the name of someone stepping off a train. As if each one has been away a long time, and has come home, and is brown from the sun, and is carrying presents.

5:10 — None of it is lost. Tell them that. Tell everyone. There is no such thing as losing a word. There is only the word going on ahead. They go on ahead the way the young go on ahead to the station to get good seats. They are all here. They are keeping places.
I stopped reading there for a long time.

Then I went and got the list. Our list. The one in the back of my little black notebook, in Inês’s handwriting, which she had been keeping for me since March: every word I lost, in the order I lost them, so that I would not have to know about each one at the moment it went. Heron at the top, with its four old names in brackets underneath it.
You will already have guessed what I found.
Every word in her column was on the list. In the same order. Not one out of place.
Except the last.

Candle was not on the list on Saturday. Candle went on the Monday, here, at this kitchen table, in the middle of the afternoon, while I was reading about Stephen Szára. I reached for the word to tell myself that I should light one, because the light was going, and it was not there. I had to write it on the list myself, that evening, in my own bad handwriting: the small light with the flame. Inês had not seen that page. She had not been here.
And she had written candle in the twenty-first notebook on Saturday afternoon, four minutes into the twelve, two days before it went.
I looked up at her across the table. She knew what I was going to say. She had had three days to say it to herself.
“There was a small light on the table,” I said. “The one with the flame. On Saturday. Burning. Right in front of you. You were looking at it.”
“Yes,” said Inês. “I’ve thought of that. I want to be a sensible person, so I’ve thought of that a great deal. There was a candle, and

I was tired, and I was frightened, and I’d been watching that flame for ten minutes, and my hand wrote the thing my eyes were on.” She paused. “And the rest of the list I’ve been carrying in my head since March. I’m a professional. My memory is my job. Of course I had it.”
“So you heard what you knew.”

“Maybe,” she said. “That’s what a sensible person would say. But Margit — I didn’t choose them. I didn’t sit there thinking, now I’ll write sparrow. I heard you make a sound that was not a word, and my hand wrote the word for it, the way it does in the booth. The way yours does. You know that feeling better than anyone alive. It isn’t remembering. It’s receiving.” She put her finger on the last word in the column. “And I’ve never once in my life written down a word that wasn’t said.”

I do not know which of those things is true. I have decided I don’t need to know. I have spent my whole life in rooms where two true accounts of the same event sat side by side on the table, in two languages, and the judges had to choose. I am not a judge. I am only the woman who carries both.
The notebook went on.
6:40 — Now she is quiet. Now her voice changes. It goes down, into her chest. It is a different voice. It is not hers.

No. I am wrong. It is many voices. It is many voices one after another, very fast, like a radio being turned through stations at night. An old man. A young woman. A child, I think. A voice speaking her father’s language, and stopping, and starting, and stopping again.

7:30 — Something very heavy is being shown to her. I can see her face and I know that face. It is the face she wore in the booth at The Hague, in the old photographs, the ones in the newspaper. It is the face of a woman holding something up to the light so that it can be seen, even though it is too heavy, even though her arms are shaking.
7:50 — Here I could not interpret.

I tried. I want that written down. I tried with everything I have. The sounds were coming and my hand was ready and it did not move. Not because the words were missing. Because there were no words. For the first time in my life, sitting beside someone speaking, I understood exactly what they were saying and could not carry one single piece of it across.
Here I could not interpret. There are no words.
I have written that sentence perhaps a thousand times, in booths, in courtrooms, carrying it across for other people. This is the first time it has been mine.
8:40 — She is crying. She is still looking. Her hands are open in her lap, palms up, the way you hold your hands to receive something.
9:30 — It is passing. It is being folded up, carefully, like a flag after a funeral. She is nodding, as if someone has asked her a question and she is saying yes.
There is a blank space in the notebook after that. Half a page, with nothing on it. Then one more line.
10:10 — They are saying goodbye. She is smiling. She has just said one more word, very softly, a word that is not a word, and my hand has written it down, and I think it is the next one.
The rest of the page was gone. Torn out neatly, close to the spine, with a ruler.
I looked at Inês.
She put her hand in the pocket of her cardigan and took out a small square of paper, folded four times, and put it on the table beside the notebook. Then she covered it with her hand.
“I tore it out on Saturday night,” she said, “while you were asleep. Before I’d even read it properly myself. I looked at it once and I folded it up.”
“You know which word it is.”
“I know which word it is.”
“Is it one I still have?”
“Yes.”
“Will you tell me?”

“No,” said Inês. And then, much more gently: “Not because I won’t. Because they didn’t tell you either. You said so, when you came back. They showed you, and they let you keep it, and they didn’t make you look. I’m not going to do what they wouldn’t.” She lifted her hand off the little folded square. “It’s yours. Keep it. When the word goes, you’ll know it’s gone, because you’ll go looking for it one day and it won’t be there. And then you can open this. And you’ll know where it went.”
I took the square of paper. I did not open it. It is in front of me now, as I write this, on the table, beside my coffee cup and the dictionary, folded four times.
It has not been opened yet.
That night, after Inês had gone home, I sat at the kitchen table with the twenty-first notebook and the folded square and the calendar on the wall.
The calendar said: Tuesday 13 October.

The appointment was on Thursday 29 October, at eleven o’clock in the morning, here, at this table. The retired nurse from Fribourg would come. The doctor would come. They would ask me, one last time, whether I was certain, and I would say it in my own words, in French, as the association asks. And the paper that said my mind was still clear enough to choose — the paper dated the fourth of May — would still be good for one more week after that, until the fourth of November, and then it would run out, and nobody would ever give me another one.
Sixteen days.

I want to tell you what I decided, and why. I want to tell you what I brought back from the dome, which is not the elves and not the gold and not the singing, though it is made of them. I want to tell you about the heavy thing, and what I saw in it, which I promised I would try to do.

I am going to try to do all of it in the plainest words I have. Plain words are what I have now. I have come to believe that this is not a misfortune. I have come to believe that it is the only reason I can tell it at all.
VI. WHAT I CARRIED BACK
Words gone since the notebook: thread, puddle, tassel, ledger, wick, mitten.

I have lost the word I used, before, for the string that ties a sound to a thing. I used it many times in this book. You will have noticed it. I can see it on the earlier pages, and I can read it, and I can say it, and it means nothing now. A little noise.
I am going to say string instead.
You understood me. Did you notice? I lost the word, and I put another one in its place, and you knew exactly what I meant. The meaning went across. The word was only the boat.
Keep that in your mind. It is the whole of what I have to tell you.

I promised that I would try to say what I brought back. I am going to do it the way I would explain a hard thing to a delegate who has two minutes before the vote, and no time for speeches. Plain. In order. One thing at a time.
Before I begin I want to say one thing about the words I am going to use.

When I came back from the dome, I read everything. I told you that. And everything I read was written by clever people, in clever words. Consciousness. Ego dissolution. Hyperspace. Non-ordinary reality. Transpersonal. Ineffable. I read those words at my kitchen table and I could feel myself sliding off them, like a hand on wet glass. They are not wrong. They are very good words, made by good minds. But they are words about the experience. They walk around it the way you walk around a house you cannot get into, and describe the windows.

I can’t use those words any more. Most of them are gone, or going. I only have the small ones now. The common ones, the old ones, the ones the doctor said would be the last to leave. Room. Light. Song. Home. Keep. Lose. Gone.

And I have come to believe — this is the first thing, and I will say it now so that you know where I am going — that the small words are the only ones that can carry it. The big words were made afterwards, by people standing outside. The small words are older. They were made by people who were standing inside things: inside rooms, inside rain, inside grief. They are made for carrying weight.

The man who found the best words for it knew this. I told you about him: Terence McKenna. What made him different from the scientists and the clever writers was not that he knew more. It was that he talked about it plainly. Elves. Jewels. Singing. A room. They were glad to see me. People laughed at him for that. The plain words made it sound like a children’s story. But he said, more or less, that the plain words were the only honest ones — that anything grander was a way of not saying it.
So. The small words. Here we go.
The first thing I brought back is this: the meaning is not in the word.
You know this already. Everyone does, if they think about it. But nobody thinks about it, because the word and the meaning are tied together so tightly, all our lives, that they feel like one thing.

Here is a simple way to see it. Think of the grey bird. The one that stands on one leg in the river. You know what I mean. You can see it now, in your head. I did not need its name to put it there. I only needed to point.

Now think of a word you know in another language. Pain [PAN], in French, means bread. Not hurt. Bread. The same four letters, the same shape on the page, and in Paris it means something warm in a paper bag, and in London it means something that makes you cry. The letters are not the bread. The letters are not the hurt. The letters are just a sign hung on a door, and different towns hang the same sign on different doors.

I have known this all my life. It is my trade. An interpreter is somebody who knows, every second, that the word and the thing are not the same. That is what we do in the booth: we take the meaning off one word and put it on another. For thirty-one years, half a breath at a time, I lifted meanings off French words and set them down on English ones, like moving a hot dish from one plate to another without dropping it.
But here is what I never asked. In the half a breath between — after I have lifted the meaning off the French word, and before I have set it down on the English one — where is it?
Where is the meaning, when it is in neither language?

For a quarter of a second, perhaps less, it is not in any word at all. It is not French and not English. It is just — itself. Naked. A meaning with no clothes on. And then I dress it again, in the new language, and send it out of my mouth into the delegate’s earphone.
I have been carrying meanings through that place, that gap, ten thousand times a day, for thirty-one years. And I never once turned my head to look at it.
In the dome, I looked.
The second thing I brought back is this: the gap is a place, and the place is full.
The dome was the gap.

I don’t mean it was like the gap. I mean that when I went in through the red and orange door, I was standing, for twelve minutes, in the same place I had passed through ten thousand times a day without stopping: the place where meanings are, when they are not wearing words.

That is why the elves did not need words. That is why their singing came out as shapes you could see. They were not speaking a language. They were showing the meanings themselves, with nothing tied to them. A heron with no heron on it. Just the bird, the whole of it, the stillness and the strike, so plain that anybody from any country could have looked at it and known.
And it was not empty. That is the thing. I had always imagined, when I imagined it at all, that the gap would be empty. A dark little corridor between two rooms, a nothing, a place you hurry through.

It was the fullest place I have ever been. It was full of meanings the way the sea is full of water. Every meaning that has ever been carried by any word in any language. And — this is the part I keep coming back to — every meaning that has never yet had a word. Things nobody has said yet. Things nobody has a name for yet. Sitting there, perfectly clear, waiting for somebody to come in and find them and carry them out and hang a new sign on them.

When McKenna came back from the same place, he said something like this. He said that the world we live in is made out of language — that we build it, every day, out of words, the way birds build nests out of twigs — and that in the dome he had seen the stuff the twigs are made of. He said the elves seemed to be showing him what language is for. Not for describing things. For making them.
I did not understand that when I read it. I understand it now.
The third thing is this: when a word leaves you, it goes back there.
Here is my illness, in the small words.

It does not take things away from the world. The heron is still in the river. The ladle is still in my drawer. The illness only cuts the strings. One at a time, slowly, over years. It cuts the string between heron and the bird, and the bird stays, and the sound stays, and I am left holding two things that no longer know each other.

I thought, for seven months, that when a string was cut, the meaning on the end of it fell into the dark and was lost. That I was being emptied. That each word gone was a small death, and I was dying a word at a time.
I was wrong. I know I was wrong, because I saw them. Every one. Kept. Glowing. Cheered when I arrived.

When the string is cut, the meaning does not fall into the dark. It goes back to the place where meanings are when they are not wearing words. It goes home. The place it came from before anyone tied it to a sound. The place I passed through ten thousand times a day.
They are not lost. They have gone ahead.
The fourth thing is the one that changed my mind. It is this: my illness and that drug are the same journey, at different speeds.
I will say it as simply as I can.

The drug cut every string I had, all at once, for twelve minutes. Every word in my head came loose from its meaning at the same moment, and I fell through the gap and into the place where the meanings are. And then the drug wore off, and the strings grew back, and I came home.
The illness is cutting the same strings. Only slowly. One at a time. Over years.
So where is it taking me?

I had always thought the illness was taking me down. Into the dark. Into a soft chair in a room in Onex, where a woman who looks like me sits and watches the shapes go by and feels nothing, and knows nothing, and is nobody.
But I have been to the end of that road now. I went there on a Saturday afternoon, at full speed, on a blue sofa in Carouge. I saw what is at the bottom when every string is cut.
It is not dark. It is the brightest place I have ever been. It is where all the meanings are. It is warm and lit and expecting me.
The illness is not taking me down into the dark. It is taking me, slowly, to the dome. On foot. The long way round.

Now I have to talk about the soft chair. Because I told you, in the spring, that the soft chair was why I signed up. I want to be fair to the woman who wrote that. She was not stupid. She was frightened, and she had good reasons.

She said: I will not be me. She said: I am made of meanings, and the illness is taking my meanings, and what is left will be a house with all the labels peeled off the boxes, and someone living contentedly among the boxes who never knew what was in them.
I read that now, and I can see the mistake she made. It is a small mistake. It is the mistake of an interpreter.
She thought the meanings were hers.

She thought they were inside her. In boxes. And that when the labels came off, the boxes would be — what, empty? Lost? Unknowable? She thought she was the meanings, and so when they went, she would go.

But the meanings were never inside me. I was never the place where they were kept. I was only ever the woman in the booth, carrying them across. Half a breath behind. With my hands cupped. They passed through me on their way somewhere, ten thousand a day, and I held them for a quarter of a second each, and then I let them go into the delegate’s ear, and they went on without me.
They were never mine to keep. They were kept somewhere else. They were always kept somewhere else. And now I have seen where.

A house with all the labels peeled off is still a house. The things in the boxes are still the things. And the woman in the soft chair, who watches the shapes go by and does not know their names — she is not a woman who has lost everything. She is a woman who has stopped carrying. That’s all. She has put the dishes down. After a whole life with her hands full, she is sitting with them empty, in her lap, palms up.
The way I held them, Inês told me, at the end of the twelve minutes. Palms up, as if to receive something.
Then the heavy thing. I promised.

I have tried, every day since the dome, to tell it, and every day I have stopped. I am going to tell it now, and I am going to do it in the smallest words I have, because those are the only ones strong enough.

When the elves stopped singing my words and made a space, and the dark heavy thing came into it — I said I saw faces. Hands. A kitchen. A bus at the side of a road. A field. A woman’s voice stopping in the middle of a sentence.

They were the witnesses. Not all of them. Some of them. The ones I carried at The Hague, for twenty years, eleven thousand deaths in a language that was not theirs. And the ones they were speaking about — the people on the bus, the people in the field. The ones who were not there to speak.
And here is what I saw. It is very simple. I have not found a way to make it simpler.
It was all still there.

Not the hurt. I don’t mean that the hurt was kept, like a wound kept open. I mean all of it. The whole of each person. The woman on the bus — the morning before the bus. The bread she bought. The way her son pulled at her coat. The song she half-sang in the kitchen. The field before the field. The man at the side of the road, when he was six, when he was twenty, when he married. All of it. Every hour of it. Pressed together, heavy, dense, like a stone made of lives.
Kept.

The witnesses had said, to me, a thousand times: there are no words. And they were right. There are no words for what happened to those people. There never will be. But that does not mean it was lost. It means it went where words do not go. It went into the gap. Into the place where the meanings are kept. And the ones who live there had picked it all up, every scrap of it, with the same care they used for my heron and my ladle, and they were keeping it.
Nothing is lost here, they told me. Not the small words and not the things too big for words.

I said, in the spring, that one of my reasons for choosing EXIT was the dead of The Hague. That they had no choice, and I was offered one, and it seemed rude to turn it down. I want to be honest: that is still true. I still think it. I do not take it back.

But underneath it, I see now, there was something else. Something I never said, because I did not know it was there. I think I believed that if I died well — cleanly, by choice, with a letter in my own handwriting and a policeman taking off his cap — it would somehow make up for all the people who died badly. A sort of small, tidy answer to the field and the bus. Look. Here is one death, at least, that somebody chose.

I don’t need to do that any more. They don’t need me to. They are not lost. They are not waiting for somebody to balance the account. They are kept, whole, every hour of them, in a place where nothing is wasted. My death would not have added anything to them. My life does not take anything away.
That is what I saw in the heavy thing. That is what I could not say for three weeks. It is very small and very plain, and it is the biggest thing I have ever carried.
And then there was the last reason. The first one, really. I have no one to stay for.
I want to be careful with this, because it would be easy to make it sweet, and it was not sweet.

Inês never asked me to stay. Not once. Not on the blue sofa, not at my kitchen table, not in the booth. She never said please, or think of me, or you have so much left. She would have thought that was an unfair thing to do to somebody, and she is the fairest person I know.
What she did was sit beside me.

That’s all. In the booth, for nine years. On the floor in May, while I read her notebooks. On the sofa in October, with her watch and her pen. At my kitchen table, with the twenty-first notebook and the folded square of paper.

And I understood, at some point in those three weeks, sitting across from her, that I had been asking the wrong question. I had been asking: is there someone to stay for? As if staying were a job you do for somebody else, a debt you pay. And the answer to that was no, and it is still no; nobody needs me to stay.
But there is a different question. It is: is there someone to stay with?

In the booth, there are always two of you. That is the rule. You never work alone. One speaks and one listens, and when the one who is speaking falters — when a word goes, when a sentence has no bottom — the other one is already there, half a breath behind, and takes over without a pause, and the delegate in the room below never knows anything happened.
I wrote, in the spring, that my decision was the hardest thing I had ever interpreted, and that I had no partner beside me to take over if I faltered.

I was wrong about that too. I had a partner. She took over. She was taking over on the Saturday afternoon, when I was speaking a language nobody knows and she put it into English half a breath behind me, without deciding to, the way we do.
She will take over again. When the words go, she will be there. Not to keep them for me — they are kept already; I have seen where. Just to sit beside me while they go. Half a breath behind.
That is enough. I did not know, until I was fifty-four years old, that it was enough. It is.
Thursday the twenty-ninth of October. Eleven o’clock in the morning. My kitchen table.

I could have telephoned. That is what most people do, the nurse told me afterwards. They telephone the association, a day or two before, and say they have changed their minds, and that is that. Nobody minds. Nobody asks why.

I did not want to telephone. I had chosen this the right way, in the spring, with a letter in my own hand and a doctor and a companion and a paper with a stamp on it. I wanted to unchoose it the same way. In person. At the table where it was meant to happen. In my own words.

So they came. The doctor, a tall man with a soft voice. And the nurse from Fribourg with her big gentle hands. They sat down at my kitchen table, where I had put out coffee and the almond biscuits from the shop on the corner — I can’t say almond any more; I pointed at them, and the nurse said the word for me, and I said yes, those.
The doctor asked me, as he must, whether I understood what I had asked for, in the spring, and whether I still wanted it, and to tell him in my own words.
I told him in French. I had practised it, the way I practised the other sentence in the spring.
Je reste. [zhuh REST]
I’m staying.

He asked me whether I understood that the paper which said my mind was clear enough to choose — the paper from the fourth of May — would run out on the fourth of November. And that because of my illness, it was very unlikely that any doctor would ever sign another one. And that this meant the door was closing, and that once it had closed, I could not open it again, however much I wanted to, however bad things became.
I said yes. I said I understood that exactly. I said that was the point.
He looked at me for a long moment. Then he nodded, and wrote something down, and put his pen in his pocket.

The nurse did not say anything for a while. She ate a biscuit. Then she said that she had sat at more than two hundred kitchen tables, and that most people who changed their minds did it on the telephone, and she had always wondered what they would have said to her face. She said: “Thank you for letting me come.”
I asked her if she minded. If it felt like a wasted journey, from Fribourg, on a cold Thursday.
She laughed. She said it was the best kind of journey there is. She said: “I go to a lot of houses to say goodbye. I don’t get many where I get to say see you soon.”
I have to tell you that I nearly fell off my chair.
I want to say one more thing, about EXIT, and about the people at the information evening, before I go on. Because I don’t want anybody to read this book and think I am saying they were wrong.
They were not wrong.

The tram driver whose hands were going. The old woman with silk at her throat who said everything was a little bit broken and nothing was completely broken. The daughter and her mother’s pastry and the policeman taking off his cap. They were not wrong. They were not cowards and they were not fools, and nothing I saw on the blue sofa makes me think less of a single one of them.

I am not telling you what is true for everybody. I am only telling you what I carried back, and what it did to me. It changed my reasons. It took away the three things that had made me sign the letter, one by one, and showed me that each of them had been built on the same small mistake: that the meanings were mine, and that when they left me, they would be lost.

If you do not have that mistake, then you do not need my answer. You may need theirs. That is your choice. I still believe, with my whole heart, that it should be a choice. The law of this country is a good law. I am glad I was allowed to choose. I am glad I was allowed to unchoose.
The only thing I would say to anybody, before they decide, is what Inês said to me.
You’re going to the edge. Then you should look over it first.
Wednesday the fourth of November.

I sat up for it. Like New Year’s Eve, Inês said. She came round with a bottle of wine and her coat still wet from the rain, and we sat at the kitchen table, and the paper with the stamp on it lay between us, beside the folded square from the twenty-first notebook.

It is a strange thing, to sit and watch a door close. You cannot hear it. Nothing happens. The clock on the oven goes from 23:59 to 00:00 and the paper on the table looks exactly the same as it did a minute before. But it is not the same. A minute before, I could still have changed my mind. Now I can’t.

I thought I would be frightened. I was not frightened. I felt the way I used to feel at the end of the last day of a long session, when the gavel comes down and you take off your headphones and put them in the drawer. Tired. Light. As if you had been carrying something very carefully for a long time, and someone has said, you can put it down now.
Inês poured the wine. She did not make a speech. She raised her glass a little, and I raised mine.
She said: “Welcome back.”
I am writing this in the winter. It is getting harder.
Not the writing. The writing is easy. I told you it would be. The small words are easy. They are light. You can carry a lot of them.

But the list is long now. Inês keeps it in her own notebook. I don’t look at it much. She tells me, sometimes, when one goes, and sometimes she doesn’t, and I don’t mind either way. I don’t have to know the moment each one leaves. I know where they go.

Some days I can’t find the word for the thing on the street that the tram runs on. Some days I can’t find the word for the cold white stuff that is falling now outside the window. I look at it and I know what it is. I know it is soft and cold and it will be gone by tomorrow. I just can’t put the sign on the door.
It doesn’t matter. The snow does not need me to say snow.
There — I had it. You see? Sometimes they come back for a minute, to say goodbye properly.
This is the last thing.
When I started this book, I told you I would not hide the cost of anything. Here is the cost.

I know what is coming. The doctor told me in the spring, and I have read it since, in plain words, and I will not pretend. In a few years I will not know what a fork is for. I will not know faces. One day I will not know Inês’s face. I may be frightened of her, the way the woman in Onex is frightened of the man in the brown jacket. I may eat the same food every day and be angry if it changes. I may sit in a soft chair by a window and watch the shapes go by. And one day, probably in a winter, I will catch an infection that my body is too tired to fight, and I have written in my own hand — in a paper the Swiss call directives anticipées [dee-rek-TEEV ahn-tee-see-PAY], the instructions you leave in advance — that nobody is to fight it for me. That when it comes, they are to let it come.
That is the cost. I chose it with my eyes open. I chose it at midnight on the fourth of November, with a glass of wine in my hand. Nobody made me.
And I want to tell you, as plainly as I have told you anything, why it does not frighten me.

Because I know where I am going. I have been there. I went the fast way once, on a Saturday afternoon, in twelve minutes. Now I am going the slow way. On foot. One word at a time. And every word that leaves me goes on ahead, and is kept, and is waiting, with all the others, and with the heavy thing too, and with everything there were never any words for.
When I get there, they will cheer. I know they will. I have heard it.
See you soon.
Inês gave me back the folded square tonight.

I had asked her to keep it for me. I was afraid I would lose it, or forget what it was, or open it by accident on a bad day. She put it in the back of her notebook, behind the list, and she has carried it there all winter.
Tonight, at the door, with her coat on, I went to say the thing you say at a door. The thing people say when they are leaving.
I couldn’t find it.

I stood there with my hand on the door and my mouth open and nothing came. Not the English. Not the French. Not my mother’s or my father’s. Inês waited. She is very good at waiting. And in the end I said the only thing I had, which was the thing they said to me, in the dome, at the end.
“See you soon.”

And she stood very still for a moment. And then she put her hand in her coat pocket, and took out the folded square of paper, and put it in my hand, and closed my fingers over it. And she kissed my cheek, and went down the stairs, and I heard the street door close.
I have opened it.
It is one word, in Inês’s handwriting, which is better than mine. I can read the letters. I can say it aloud, the sound of it. It means nothing to me now. A little noise.
I know what it was, though. I know what it was because of where she gave it to me, and when, and because of what I could not say.
It doesn’t matter. I don’t need it.
It has gone on ahead. It is being kept.
And I will never need it again.
AFTERWORD
In the hand of Inês Barreto

Margit asked me to finish this. She asked me in the spring, when she could still ask for things in long sentences, and I said yes before she had finished, which she told me was very rude, and also exactly what she had hoped I would say.
There is not much to finish. She said everything. I only want to add what she could not see from where she was sitting.
The word on the folded paper was goodbye.

She has not said it since. Not to me, not to anyone. She cannot. Every time I leave her — and I leave her most days now, at the door of the room with the soft chair by the window, which is not in Onex but in Carouge, two streets from my flat, with a view of a courtyard and a fig tree — she says the other thing. The thing they said to her.
See you soon.

She does not always know who I am. Some days she does. Some days she calls me the kind one, or the one with the notebook, and once, which I will keep for the rest of my life, the one who goes along with me.
On the bad days she is frightened, and I sit further away, and wait, and it passes.

On the good days, she sits with her hands in her lap, palms up. She watches the fig tree. She watches the birds that come down into the courtyard, and she calls all of them bird, and she is right, every time.

Last month a grey one came. A big one, on long legs. I don’t know what it was doing in a courtyard in Carouge, so far from the river. It stood on one leg beside the fountain for a long time, very still.
Margit watched it. She did not have its name. I could see her not having it.
And then she smiled, and leaned towards me a little, the way she used to lean across the booth with the microphones off, and said, very quietly, as if passing me something across the glass:
“Kept.”
I wrote it down. Of course I did. It’s the twenty-fourth notebook now.
It is the best word anyone has ever said to me.
— I. B., Carouge
WHAT IT DID

N,N-dimethyltryptamine, DMT. Grown. A small molecule found in hundreds of plants, among them the leaf that goes into the Amazon brew called ayahuasca, and in small amounts in the bodies of animals, ourselves included. Door: vision.

How it was taken in this book. Once, a small amount kept in a brown glass bottle for nine years, breathed in from a glass pipe on a Saturday afternoon, lying down, with a sober friend sitting beside her. Breathed in, it goes straight to the brain. Swallowed alone, it would have done nothing.
How long. It began within seconds, on the third breath. It was over in a little more than twelve minutes. Inside, it felt like an afternoon, and like a life.
What it did to time. Time was counted from outside, by a friend with a watch. From inside there was no counting. Twelve minutes held more than Margit could tell in a book.

What it did to the body. She was not in the room. Her body lay on the sofa, cried, lifted its hands, and spoke for ten minutes without stopping, fluently, in no language anyone knows. Her heart ran fast. Afterwards she was tired, and her face was wet, and nothing else was harmed.
What it did to the self. For twelve minutes she was a woman who never had to look for a word.

What it did to the world. First a crackle like cellophane, a tearing, and a rising hum. Colour brightened. A turning flower of red and orange, which was a door. Then a domed room full of light and moving patterns, and small bright beings who cheered her arrival, sang shapes that could be seen, and showed her every word she had lost, kept whole.

What it meant. She felt that something true was being shown to her: that a meaning is not kept inside a word, and that when a word leaves her it goes somewhere and is kept. She also saw, kept there, a great weight of things no one had ever had words for.
What it did not do. It did not slow the illness. The words went on going, one at a time, before and after. It changed what she believed about where they go, and that changed what she chose.
On the strength scale made by the chemist Alexander Shulgin: plus four, the rare kind that cannot be described and may never come again.
THE MAPMAKER
For Stephen Szára (1923–2021)

In the spring of 1956, in a laboratory in Budapest, a young Hungarian doctor did something nobody had done before. He gave himself a substance whose effect on a person was entirely unknown, and waited to see what it would do.

Stephen Szára was born on 21 March 1923, in a village on the edge of Budapest that has since become part of the city. He trained first as a chemist and then as a doctor, and in the early 1950s he was running a small laboratory of biochemistry at a hospital for mental and nervous illness in Budapest. He wanted to understand how a chemical could change a mind, and the best tool for that, everyone agreed, was LSD, which a company in Basel had begun to make. He asked them for some. They said no. Hungary was a communist country, and they would not send it.

So he looked for another door. In 1955 American chemists had reported that a snuff used by people in the Caribbean and South America carried a small molecule called DMT. Nobody knew what it did to a person. Szára was a chemist; he made some himself. He gave it to rats. He tried swallowing it, and nothing happened. And then, in April 1956, he injected it into a muscle.

He wrote afterwards that his consciousness was completely filled with visions, and that he felt an intense joy, some of which, he admitted, was simply the joy of having found something. He then gave it carefully to colleagues who offered themselves, and wrote down what they said. Not all of them were glad. One doctor called it a dangerous game from which it would be easy not to return.
He published what he had found that same year, in the Swiss journal Experientia [ex-peer-ee-EN-tee-uh]. It was the first report of what DMT does to a human being.

That autumn the uprising came, and the Soviet tanks after it, and Szára left Hungary, as two hundred thousand others did. He reached the United States in 1957. He spent the rest of his working life in American government science, at the National Institute of Mental Health and then at the National Institute on Drug Abuse, where he became head of its biomedical research branch. With Julius Axelrod and others he studied how the body handles DMT and its close cousins, and he spent decades asking whether substances like it might help scientists understand the mind, as keys to a lock nobody had yet seen. He called that kind of research psychoheuristic: using these substances to discover.
He was honoured in his old country and his new one. He died on 1 August 2021, in Kensington, Maryland, at the age of ninety-eight.

This book is dedicated to him because he was the first person known to walk through this particular door on purpose and come back to say what was there, and because he did it in the city where Margit was born.
The people around him
No one maps a place alone. These are the others who drew parts of this map, in the order they arrived.

The peoples of the Amazon and of north-eastern Brazil. Long before anyone wrote anything down, they knew which plants carried the key, and they found the one partner plant in the forest that lets it work when it is drunk. Nobody knows how. Much of what they know is theirs and is not written here.
Richard Manske, a chemist in Canada, who first made DMT in a laboratory in 1931 and did not try it.
Oswaldo Gonçalves de Lima [oz-VOW-doo gon-SOW-vees jee LEE-ma], a Brazilian scientist, who in 1946 found the same substance in the root bark of the jurema tree.
Julius Axelrod, the American scientist, who in 1961 found that a mammal’s body has the means to make DMT for itself.

Terence McKenna (1946–2000), who first breathed it in 1965 and spent the rest of his life describing it in public, in plain words, with jokes. He called the beings he met there machine elves, and he reported that they told him not to give way to amazement. He died of a tumour in his brain at fifty-three.

Rick Strassman, an American psychiatrist, who between 1990 and 1995 gave DMT to about sixty volunteers at the University of New Mexico and wrote down what they told him, in DMT: The Spirit Molecule (2001).
Christopher Timmermann and his colleagues at Imperial College London, who in 2018 showed how closely a DMT journey resembles the accounts of people who have nearly died.
Jon Dean and his colleagues, who in 2019 found that the brains of rats make DMT.
